The deployment illustrates how multidimensional treatment modeling and observational pretraining, combined with adaptation using RCT data, can support effective joint discount decisions in production.

title: OceanTensorCube and ST-MMT: A Multimodal Data and Transformer System for Seven-Day Forecasting of Pyropia Bleaching
comments: 27 pages. Forecasting service: this https URL
abstract: Bleaching of cultured Pyropia (laver) causes losses in Korean seaweed farming. We present a system that forecasts bleaching seven days ahead for farm clusters. OceanTensorCube aligns 32 channels from public marine, meteorological, ocean-model and satellite sources on a 30 m grid, and ST-MMT, a 9.2-million-parameter spatiotemporal transformer with hub-style multi-head cross-attention between variable groups, maps a 14-day input window to a seven-day-ahead bleaching probability. On the validation set, a six-seed ensemble detects every reported positive at a false-alarm rate of at most 3.5%, an upper bound because the report-based labels are positive-unlabeled. A same-date control on separately trained models indicates that the architecture discriminates between clusters when the calendar is held fixed. We also report the system's weaknesses: skill falls steeply as the quarterly nutrient survey ages (ROC-AUC 0.94 at 30 days, 0.53 at 129 days), and a single LSTM on cluster-average series outperforms a single ST-MMT, with only the ensemble leading at the operating point. We describe the labeling procedure, the evaluation protocol and the operational gate that withholds forecasts when inputs are stale. The forecasting service is operated at this https URL.

title: SEAM: Spectral Embedding Alignment and Merging for Low-Resource TTS
comments: Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
abstract: Expanding the vocabulary of conditional text-to-speech (TTS) models typically requires extensive fine-tuning with paired audio, creating a major bottleneck for low-resource and cross-lingual adaptation. To address this, we introduce SEAM, a zero-audio initialization method that constructs embeddings for unseen tokens from known subtokens. Unlike standard pooling strategies that ignore sequential structure, SEAM applies a spectral filter to preserve temporal phonetic order and uses closed-form ridge regression to align the new embeddings with the pretrained conditioning manifold. Across three languages and two TTS architectures, SEAM approaches or matches baseline performance using up to four times less training data, reducing sample complexity by 75\% compared to random initialization and mean pooling. Our approach provides a lightweight, reproducible, and theoretically grounded solution for vocabulary expansion in low-resource speech synthesis.

title: Trust Your Targets: Is Target Propagation Block-Diagonal Gauss-Newton?
abstract: Target propagation (TP) is a backpropagation alternative in which local targets carry the global learning signal. Prior works claim that TP performs Gauss-Newton (GN) optimisation on these targets, but the correspondence has only been established under unrealistic assumptions where hitting them exactly is trivial. Practical variants instead descend on a least-squares problem via a single gradient step. In this paper, we rederive TP from a trust region under an implicit, previously unexamined norm, and introduce CGTP (Conjugate Gradient Target Propagation), which uses conjugate gradients to solve the layer-local subproblems in parallel. A single adaptive parameter jointly controls this trust region and a matching bound on the weight update; KFAC emerges exactly as the special case where the per-sample Jacobians are replaced by their batch mean, giving its factored damping a variational grounding. On MNIST and Fashion-MNIST MLPs, CGTP matches the accuracy of ADAM and KFAC while needing orders of magnitude fewer outer iterations than ADAM (about 10x fewer backward-pass-equivalents overall), while remaining stable across depth.

title: Learning SOCP Solver Dynamics with Graph Neural Networks
comments: Learning on Graphs (LoG) Conference, 2026
abstract: Second-order cone programs (SOCPs) are a fundamental class of convex optimization problems widely applied across engineering domains. Classical interior-point methods are robust and accurate, but their iterative nature can be costly in real-time or repeated-solve settings. This has motivated learning-based solvers that approximate optimizer solutions with neural networks. Recent work has increasingly studied graph neural networks (GNNs) for linear, quadratic, and second-order cone optimization, leveraging their ability to model sparse relational structure among variables, constraints, and objective functions. Most existing GNN-based solvers compress the optimization process into a single forward pass, predicting the optimizer directly without using the intermediate trajectory produced by classical solvers. We introduce SOCPNet, a recursive GNN framework that uses solver trajectories to learn an iterative SOCP solution procedure. A shared GNN model is applied repeatedly, refining the current iterate at each step and enabling inference for a variable number of iterations. Rather than predicting the solution in a single pass, SOCPNet learns from intermediate iterates to progressively refine its estimates using a trajectory-regularized training procedure. We evaluate SOCPNet on multiple datasets spanning standard SOCP problem classes and show that it consistently reduces the final solution error relative to a SOCP-GNN baseline. Finally, we demonstrate how trained SOCPNet models can be used in a hybrid optimization pipeline by warm-starting a classical interior-point solver, reducing solver iterations without loss of accuracy.

title: CAST: Cast-Admissible Generative Design and Shape Optimization with Paired Depth Images
abstract: Deep generative design can produce complex geometries, but unconstrained representations may create undercuts that prevent release from a two-part mold. We present CAST, which reformulates three-dimensional shape generation under a selected mold-opening constraint as a two-dimensional image generation problem using paired top and bottom depth images. Each valid depth pair defines one material interval along a selected mold-opening direction, so reconstructions exclude undercuts in that direction by construction. Diffusion models generate candidate shapes in this representation, and a finite element analysis (FEA) guided optimizer refines the same two boundaries. We evaluate diffusion-based generation with limited training data comprising 211 SimJEB bracket designs. On SimJEB brackets, FEA-guided refinement with a volume penalty reduced compliance in 193 of 200 generated candidates. The median reduction across all candidates was 36.8 percent in the optimization FEA model. Reconstruction of existing brackets revealed a mass--stiffness trade-off: filling occluded regions increased material volume and reduced displacement under the evaluated loads. Paired depth images thus connect generative exploration and structural refinement in a shared design space that preserves the selected pull-direction restriction.

title: Typed Decision Models under Prevalence Shift: Decision Training, Calibration, and Implicit Priors
comments: 27 pages, 5 figures. Code, protocol and per-example outputs: this https URL
abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs) return a probability over caller-defined options, and Jev is described by its vendor as calibrated. But in deployment class frequencies change, so calibration measured on a fixed test set need not hold where thresholds are applied. Existing evaluations leave two gaps: the gains of vendor decision training have not been separated from those of the backbone under an identical readout, and TDMs have been tested only at the test set's class distribution. We ask whether decision training improves a model over its own backbone, and whether a TDM's calibration and thresholds withstand prevalence (label) shift as well as a fine-tuned classifier's. We compare three TDMs (Jev, Tev1-4B, Nimble-9B), their base models and two trained classifiers on identical decisions from five public datasets under simulated shift, with 35 paired tests fixed before any test was computed. First, decision training is not uniformly beneficial: Nimble-9B, which differs from Qwen3.5-9B only by a LoRA adapter, is better calibrated on intent tasks but 12.0 Macro-F1 points worse on financial sentiment. Second, under moderate shift Jev's expected calibration error (ECE) and threshold risk grow significantly more than a fine-tuned DeBERTa's only on financial sentiment, by 1.7 and 2.5 percentage points; averaged over 2,000 shift scenarios (exploratory), the gap is at most one point on every dataset. Third, EM prior correction with the model's mean development prediction as its prior needs no labels and lowers Jev's ECE under shift by 2.7 and 1.8 points on the two datasets where it is highest, although labelled recalibration lowers it far more. The three TDMs we tested are neither uniformly better than their backbones nor uniquely fragile under shift; for calibration, their main weakness is the miscalibration they already have without shift. We release all inputs, code and outputs.

title: CIS-Transolver: A Cross-Layer Incremental-State Neural Operator for Fine-Scale Automotive Aerodynamic Flow Prediction
abstract: Neural operators offer an efficient data-driven approach to rapid prediction of complex automotive aerodynamic flows. However, spectral bias and other factors limit accurate reconstruction of fine-scale flow variations near complex geometries. Existing studies improve the representation and fitting of fine-scale information mainly through information extraction and training objectives. Further study is needed to determine how extracted local details can be used continually in subsequent operator computations and contribute effectively to the overall flow-field representation. We propose CIS-Transolver, a cross-layer incremental-state neural operator that extends fine-scale modeling from local information extraction to its use across layers. The method extracts fine-scale information through local multiscale analysis and encodes it as geometric moment states that are propagated and updated across layers. By combining information from previous layers with feedback to the value representations in Physics-Attention, the method allows local details to contribute continually to subsequent modeling of global physical correlations. We systematically evaluate CIS-Transolver on three public automotive aerodynamics benchmarks, ShapeNet-Car, AhmedML, and DrivAerNet++, covering surface pressure fields and volumetric pressure and velocity fields. CIS-Transolver achieves the lowest mean relative L2 error among the evaluated methods for all five prediction metrics across the three benchmarks. The relative error reductions average 8.72% across the five metrics compared with the best baseline for each metric, reaching 16.38% for ShapeNet-Car pressure prediction and 15.60% for AhmedML velocity prediction. These results provide a new approach to fine-scale flow prediction for complex geometries.

title: Logit Averaging During Training Sets a New State of the Art for Non-Invasive Speech BCI
abstract: Non-invasive brain-computer interfaces are in practice limited by signal-to-noise ratio, and recent state-of-the-art methods address this limitation by aggregating over repeated trials of the same stimulus. Yet multi-trial aggregation has been treated inconsistently across the literature: some work averages brain signals at the model's input, other work averages predictions at the model's output, and neither treats aggregation as an architectural choice in its own right. We provide the first systematic comparison of aggregation strategies for non-invasive neural decoding, evaluating six paradigms (including logit averaging during training and three attention-based variants we introduce) across three datasets, four tasks, and two group sizes. We find that aggregation choice matters substantially: training-time logit averaging, the simplest method we propose, outperforms all others in 6 of 7 settings. On the phoneme classification setting of the 2025 PNPL competition, it sets a new state of the art, significantly outperforming the competition winner by 17.4 absolute percentage points in balanced accuracy. We further draw a theoretical connection between logit averaging and joint ensemble training, which has been shown to underperform independent ensembling in the deep learning literature; our results call into question recent explanations of why joint ensemble training fails. Together, these findings establish multi-trial aggregation as a key design choice for non-invasive neural decoding and identify training-time logit averaging as a simple, effective default.

title: An Empirical Study of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods are critical for adapting large models under resource-constrained settings. However, as mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, which offer efficient inference at massive parameter scales, gain increasing prevalence in the community, a critical gap arising from the lack of systematic recipes for applying PEFT to MoE models. To narrow this gap, we conduct a large-scale systematic study that investigates a set of essential design recipes, including which modules should be adapted, which granularity should be used to adapt MoE modules, which PEFT method to use, and to what extent should the load-balancing objective be used, across three MoE backbones on downstream tasks and general knowledge tasks. Our experiments yield several key insights. First, adapting MoE experts alone achieves the highest downstream performance with competitive general capability retention under a comparable parameter budget. Second, native expert-weight updates offer a better downstream--retention trade-off than adapters that bypass experts or entire MoE modules. Third, LoRA and DoRA together define the strongest operating region for high downstream accuracy among the evaluated PEFT methods. Fourth, no nonzero load-balancing coefficient Pareto-dominates the zero baseline. We finally evaluate a weight-level redesign of MoE$^2$-LoRA on Qwen3. Moving its module-level bypass pool into native expert weights improves all four upstream endpoints by 2.4 to 17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters and a 3.2-point average downstream cost.

title: CTLite: Lightweight Irregular Multivariate Time Series Forecasting with Reusable Continuous-Time Summaries
abstract: Irregular multivariate time series forecasting (IMTSF) requires capturing temporal dynamics and cross-variable dependencies from sparse, asynchronous observations. Existing methods often rely on learned temporal encoders, coupling historical representation construction with model optimisation and repeatedly processing the same observations. We propose CTLite, a lightweight forecasting framework that decouples historical summarisation from learned prediction. Specifically, a parameter-free continuous-time moment encoder summarises local levels and trends at multiple temporal scales while suppressing poorly supported slope estimates. A compact readout combines damped local extrapolation with a low-rank cross-variable correction that accounts for observation freshness, target availability, and forecast horizon. Since the historical summaries are independent of trainable parameters and forecast queries, they can be reused across optimisation steps and repeated predictions for an unchanged history without altering predictions or parameter gradients. Experiments on four real-world benchmarks show that CTLite achieves the best or second-best mean MSE and MAE among the evaluated methods with only 88-2,537 trainable parameters. Under matched GPU workloads at batch size 32, CTLite reduces inference latency by 18.6-87.3% compared with the latest models, including the cost of historical encoding. Reusing summaries further reduces total runtime by approximately 52% over 16 forecast calls on the same history compared with recomputing the encoder for every call, including the initial encoding cost. The code is at: this https URL.

title: A Simple and General Approach to top-$k$ Selection
abstract: This paper considers the Bayesian top-$k$ identification problem, wherein a decision maker is tasked with selecting $k$ items from a pool of items of unknown quality. To assess the items, the decision maker adaptively allocates a fixed sampling budget, where each sample of an item yields a noisy observation of its quality, with the objective of minimizing the expected opportunity cost of the selected set. We propose an approach that allocates each batch of samples by minimizing a surrogate objective derived from an upper bound on the expected opportunity cost. The approach is general: samples can be allocated in batches, the selection size $k$ is arbitrary, and it applies to many sampling distributions. It is also simple and intuitive. We prove that the method's posterior expected opportunity cost decays at an exponential rate of at least half the best rate achievable by any sampling rule. In simulations across a wide range of settings, the method is competitive with, and often improves upon, the best existing algorithm in each setting.

title: On Learning Expand-and-Sparsify Representations
abstract: Expand-and-sparsify ($\texttt{EaS}$) representations lift an input to a much higher dimension through a linear map and keep only the $k$ largest coordinates. Existing theory builds that map at random and needs the expanded dimension to grow exponentially in the input dimension, which puts the construction out of practical reach. We ask what is gained by learning the map by gradient descent instead, and how that gain depends on how wide the expansion is. We sweep $73$ OpenML classification tasks and $48$ regression tasks under a protocol that holds the datasets, expanded dimensions, sparsity levels and splits fixed across every method, and we summarise each comparison by a median over datasets and a Wilcoxon signed rank test. We report four findings. First, learning the expansion helps most when the expansion is narrowest, and its advantage over a random map decays to nothing by the widest expansions we run, so a learned $\texttt{EaS}$ layer can be made small. Second, with the map learned, a top-$k$ representation that keeps at most a tenth of its coordinates is indistinguishable from a dense $\texttt{ReLU}$ layer of the same expanded dimension at every expansion factor we test, while GELU and SiLU are not. Third, when the representation is forced to be binary the sparse code is the better of the two, and the reason is that binarization costs it nothing while it costs the dense layer accuracy. Fourth, how sparse the representation can be is governed by how wide it is: the sparsity level that is free rises as the expansion grows, so there is no fixed limit on how sparse it can be. The regression tasks reproduce the first finding and qualify the second and third.

title: A Simple and Unified Method for Gradient-Variation Regret
abstract: Gradient-variation online learning has attracted increasing attention for its connections to game theory and optimization. It has been studied in both non-stationary online learning, which aims to minimize dynamic regret against time-varying comparator sequences, and universal online learning, which seeks to adapt to unknown loss curvature. Prior work obtained gradient-variation bounds using different techniques tailored to each setting. We propose a simple and unified method based on surrogate losses with a quadratic penalty on decision movement, yielding gradient-variation bounds in both settings. For non-stationary online learning, the method induces an optimistic-to-gradient-variation reduction, enabling a broad class of algorithms to match the rate established by Zhao et al. (2024). For universal online learning, it yields a simple algorithm that matches the optimal universal regret bounds of Yan et al. (2024) while relaxing the extended smoothness assumption. Finally, we apply our method to online games and improve on existing guarantees.

title: Wet-Biased Data Pipelines Mislead the Training and Evaluation of Generative Precipitation Nowcasting
comments: 63 pages, 7 figures and 3 tables in the main text, 11 supplementary figures and 9 supplementary tables. This work has been submitted to npj Climate and Atmospheric Science
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Atmospheric and Oceanic Physics (physics.ao-ph)
abstract: Generative models for precipitation nowcasting are trained and evaluated predominantly on wet-biased datasets, which over-represent precipitation events to emphasize rare extremes. Selecting test cases based on target observations is known to favor forecasts that match the selected distribution rather than the intended deployment distribution. We show analytically how this target-dependent sampling also shifts the conditional distribution learned by generative models. When training and test sampling match, even an ideal model learns precisely the distribution favored by evaluation, allowing the evaluation bias to conceal the training bias. Using a fixed satellite-to-radar diffusion model, we demonstrate that target-dependent test sampling can reverse the calibration assessment. The model appears under-predictive on a wet-biased test set but over-predictive on a deployment-representative test set. This result is replicated outside the model's training domain after a seven-year gap. Utilizing classifier-free guidance as an example, we demonstrate how the contradictory calibration assessment can misdirect downstream model development.

title: Strength Controls Change How Interventions Compare Across Sparse Autoencoder Codes
comments: 35 pages, 8 figures
abstract: Changing sparse autoencoder (SAE) codes can alter both intervention direction and magnitude, so comparing intervention effects requires a strength control specifying what is held equal. Norm matching and output calibration provide different controls, but whether interventions yield different effects across codes after strength matching remains unclear. We compare intervention effects under these controls for fixed feature groups in Gemma and Llama and observe: (1) Whole-patch scaling. With one coefficient per input, full-output Kullback-Leibler (KL) calibration leaves smaller mean effect gaps from the encoder-based reference intervention than total-norm matching for nonnegative least-squares (NNLS) refits. On new Llama inputs, total-norm matching loses 11 reference transfers, whereas full-output calibration preserves every transfer decision. (2) Positionwise scaling. On a small matched gender-agreement subset, positionwise norm matching leaves smaller observed mean gaps than full-output calibration. (3) Answer exclusion. Compared with unscaled NNLS, answer-excluded calibration reduces gaps in the measured subject-verb agreement comparisons but increases them for gender refits. Full-output KL calibration also reduces larger gaps for norm-matched constructed candidates, although matching coverage is incomplete in several settings. Since calibration uses the evaluated input's outputs, it serves as a diagnostic of residual disagreement.

title: A Fisher-Geometric View of Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Consolidating specialized foundation models into a unified generalist is a central goal of post-training. Two approaches are in common use: model merging, which is fast but treated as a heuristic, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation, which matches distributions but demands heavy rollout compute and suffers from cross-task gradient conflict. We show that the two are one objective seen at different orders. Within a shared basin of homologous specialists, the multi-teacher on-policy distillation objective is, to second order, exactly the Fisher-merging objective. Its minimizer is therefore the Fisher merge, a classic model-merging method given by a closed-form combination of the specialists, so merging is optimal, to second order, as a closed-form stage of distillation. Building on this identification, we propose Residual-Governed Branch-and-Merge(RGBM), a two-phase consolidation procedure. Concretely, a full-parameter Fisher merge is intractable on foundation models, so Phase~1 restricts the merge to the task-vector subspace. Extending tangent-space analyses of merging, we show that the same coefficients that mix task vectors also mix implicit rewards, which lets a residual program on unlabelled prompts solve for them. The program minimizes the worst per-domain residual and reports its energy-normalized values as the domain residual spectrum. Phase~2 lets this spectrum govern what may be added: RGBM passivates domains with low normalized residuals, trains isolated branches only for domains above the spectral gap, and writes back the admitted updates with calibrated shrinkage. On two open-source consolidation suites, the Phase~1 merge alone matches or outperforms fully trained multi-teacher distillation, and RGBM improves on it further with zero extra joint-training steps, whereas every un-gated write-back, including continued joint distillation from the merge, falls below it.

title: Bombadil: A Foundation Model for Plant Electrophysiology
comments: 25 pages, 13 figures, 11 tables
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Signal Processing (eess.SP); Quantitative Methods (q-bio.QM)
abstract: Living plants, like animals, use electrical signals to carry information about their physiological state across their body, from roots to branches. These signals can be recorded, as they are in animals, from a pair of differential extracellular electrodes inserted into signal-conducting tissue. While machine-learning models have been trained to predict specific plant stress states from these signals, each of these models has been trained for only a single task and none have been designed to transfer across tasks, species, or environments. These approaches do not allow easy scaling across the wide range of species and environments that are relevant to agriculture, forestry, and horticulture for both commercial and consumer plant care. Here we present Bombadil, a foundation model for plant electrophysiology, pretrained without labels on over 4 million hours of electrical signals recorded from 100 plant species in ten distinct environments, including laboratories, greenhouses, commercial orchards, and natural forests. In this way, Bombadil is able to learn the fundamental features of plant electrical signals across a wide array of species and environments. Then, from those same electrical signals, Bombadil tracks changes in seven physiological indicators of plant stress, even among species and stressors with no labels in training.

title: ITU-DESC: a missingness-aware machine-learning dementia risk score in the UK Biobank cohort
abstract: Background: Existing dementia risk scores rely on fixed, pre-selected features and linear models, or ignore bias from informative missingness in cohort data. Here we introduce the Istanbul Technical University Dementia Risk Score (ITU-DESC), an explainable machine-learning score for incident all-cause dementia that combines broad feature selection across roughly 8,000 candidate features with explicit control of missingness bias. Results: We studied approximately 500,000 UK Biobank participants with a median follow-up of 16.6 years. We withheld missingness patterns from the model using unconditional random hot-deck imputation. We stabilized feature selection by repeating BorutaSHAP-based feature selection with ten random-imputation seeds and selecting predictors chosen in at least eight of the ten seeds, which yielded 38 predictors. We trained a CatBoost gradient-boosted decision-tree model and evaluated it on a holdout test set of 50,041 participants. For all-cause incident dementia, ITU-DESC achieved an average precision of 0.138 (95% confidence interval 0.123-0.156) and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC AUC) of 0.853 (0.844-0.863), significantly outperforming other risk scores, including the strongest comparator, the UK Biobank Dementia Risk Prediction model (0.118 and 0.841). We identified dementia risk predictors absent from established scores, including leukocyte telomere length and liver enzymes. Conclusions: ITU-DESC is the first dementia risk score to combine broad feature selection with explicit control of missingness bias.

title: Degree Bounds for Separating Polynomial and Neural Invariants for Point Clouds
comments: 34 pages, 2 figures
abstract: Neural networks that respect the symmetries of point clouds commonly compute high-order representations of the rotation group to improve their expressivity. Such models are known to be universal, and thus able to separate any pair of point clouds, when using representations of sufficiently high order, yet no precise bound on this order, as a function of the number of points, was previously known. We establish the first quadratic lower and upper degree bounds for polynomials that separate point clouds of n points up to rotations and permutations. By showing Tensor Field Networks and MACE can express all invariant polynomials of a given degree with sufficient representation order, we additionally derive the first explicit, quadratic bound on the representation order sufficient for these architectures to be complete, replacing previous existence results with concrete guarantees. We further show that, under local regularity assumptions, point cloud separation can be achieved with a message-passing-based model using invariants whose degree depends only on the size of a local neighborhood, rather than on the size of the full point cloud. Finally, we provide counterexamples showing MACE must compute high order irreducible representations to separate locally regular point clouds.

title: Global Time-Aware Conditioning (GTC): A Mechanism for Time-Aware Pediatric Sleep Representation Learning
abstract: Sleep physiology evolves throughout the night, with changes in sleep cycles, respiratory stability, and cardiovascular dynamics. However, self-supervised learning (SSL) methods for sleep typically process short, fixed-duration windows without explicitly modeling where each window occurs within the full sleep session. We introduce Global Time-Aware Conditioning (GTC), a mechanism that complements local positional encodings by conditioning latent representations on the global time-of-sleep of each input window. We integrate GTC into three representative SSL frameworks and evaluate them on five clinically relevant tasks with extreme class imbalance across two independent pediatric cohorts. GTC generally improves F1 and AUPRC across architectures and tasks, with gains persisting under cross-cohort transfer, highlighting the value of global temporal context for sleep representation learning.

title: SleepPairNet: Learning Multimodal Pediatric Sleep Representations with Random-Pair Cross-Attention
abstract: Analyzing physiological sleep signals is important for assessing sleep quality and detecting sleep-related disorders. Learning inter-modal relationships across physiological signals can provide richer representations for downstream sleep analysis. We introduce \textbf{SleepPairNet}, a multimodal self-supervised learning (SSL) framework that learns pairwise interactions between physiological signals through cross-attention. We propose a random modality-pair selection strategy that exposes the model to diverse signal pairs during pretraining, enabling flexibility across modality combinations at test time. Pretrained on the NCH dataset, SleepPairNet outperforms the evaluated SSL baselines on all respiratory tasks while remaining competitive on EEG-related tasks, and shows even stronger results when transferred to the external CHAT dataset.

title: The Effectiveness and Durability of Pretraining Data Filtering in Protein Language Models
abstract: Pretraining filtering is one of the most common safeguards for open-weight language models. Here we study its effectiveness, durability and scalability using the ESM-2 family of protein language models. We find that filtering viral proteins from the pretraining data meaningfully degrades masked language modelling, mutation effect prediction and long-range contact prediction on viral proteins, while largely preserving performance on non-viral proteins. These effects are concentrated among proteins from human-infecting viruses, and grow as we scale models from 8M to 3B parameters. As models increase in size, we find that stringent filtering becomes more effective. However, fine-tuning on sequences from the removed viral families restores the lost performance. Although the cost to recover performance increases with model scale, even for the largest models it costs about 80 USD of H100 time. This work establishes pretraining filtering as moderately effective at selectively degrading performance on viral proteins, but not durable against fine-tuning with modest computational resources and access to relevant data.

title: Nested Shared-Operator Recursion on ARC-AGI-1: An Empirical Study of HRM, TRM and URM
abstract: Recursive reasoning models refine persistent internal states by repeatedly applying learned operators. We investigate whether adding a persistent intermediate state that integrates repeated updates of a faster state through the same operator improves predictive performance relative to each model family's baseline at matched parameter counts. We define this organisation operationally and implement it within three architectures: the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM), Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) and Universal Reasoning Model (URM). Using the official codebases on ARC-AGI-1, we compare each baseline with its parameter-matched nested variant. We evaluate held-out queries from tasks whose demonstrations were available during training. The experiments use a single-GPU budget far below the published training protocols. Under the tested conditions, nested variants show no consistent advantage in token accuracy, predictive loss or exact solving, which remains near zero for all configurations. The results therefore leave the hypothesis open. We specify a confirmatory comparison, with an informative baseline, multiple seeds, controls that isolate nesting and predefined criteria, to determine whether this organisation merits further development.

title: PACT: Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-Graphs for Dynamic Multi-Agent Combinatorial Optimization
abstract: Multi-agent approaches have been investigated recently as a means of improving the scalability of reinforcement learning for neural combinatorial optimization. Existing methods assume that all problem instance information is known upfront. However, real-world problems are often dynamic: relevant information is progressively revealed as the agents take actions (e.g., arriving at an edge in a routing problem only to discover it is untraversable). In such cases, existing methods fail to coordinate agents to explore and exploit the progressively revealed information. To address the arising coordination challenge, we introduce PACT (Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-graphs). PACT augments the environment graph with auxiliary nodes representing the plans of agents, which are connected to the resource nodes to indicate future dependencies. The proposed message-passing scheme over the augmented graph grounds inter-agent coordination in the environment and enables proactive, rather than reactive, conflict resolution. We show that PACT improves solution quality in dynamic problems relative to baselines and exhibits the best transfer to larger instances on which, remarkably, it outperforms centralized oracles with privileged access to instance uncertainty.

title: Which Model for Which Role? Cost-Efficient Pareto Recommendation for LLM Agentic Workflows
comments: Preliminary version accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Resource-Aware Agentic AI (RAAAI)
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (stat.ML)
abstract: LLM agentic workflows increasingly employ different models for specialized roles. Users may prefer different trade-offs between task quality and deployment cost, sometimes also considering latency. Finding good assignments incurs a separate search cost from evaluating multiple candidates. We introduce Cost-Coupled Gittins (CC-Gittins), a multi-objective extension of single-objective cost-aware Gittins search for Pareto recommendation. It exploits the coupling between evaluation and deployment costs: assignments that cost more to deploy also cost more to evaluate. The search alternates between seeking higher quality and lower deployment cost, reusing each evaluation to inform both searches. After each batch, CC-Gittins recommends assignments that are nondominated under uncertainty-adjusted estimates of quality and deployment cost. We evaluate CC-Gittins on eight quality--cost matrices from workflows with two to five roles and up to 1,681 candidate assignments. We also evaluate the method with latency as a third objective. Across the eight benchmarks, CC-Gittins recovers a substantial fraction of the true Pareto frontier at roughly 10% of the exhaustive-evaluation cost, and recovers most of the frontier with few false positives by 30%.

title: Parallel Language Models via Variational Decoding
abstract: Autoregressive language models emit one token per forward pass. This causes high inference latency, in particular as models are scaled up for quality. In this paper, we introduce Parallel Language Models (PLMs), which generate mutually consistent tokens in one forward pass by routing dependencies through latent auxiliary variables. PLMs are trained using a variational bound that reduces to an autoregressive loss plus a parallel decoding loss. Empirically, PLMs are on a faster and better Pareto frontier than autoregressive and discrete diffusion baselines. Pretrained PLMs achieve near-autoregressive pretraining loss on model scales of 80M to 3B parameters, and speedup follows a power law in model size. When post-trained, our 1.3B model matches or exceeds an identically trained autoregressive model on math, coding, and instruction-following benchmarks, speeding up inference $2.3\text{-}5.7\times$. Together, we show that parallel generation can be trained from a single training objective at autoregressive quality. We will make our code available at this https URL.

title: GeoSplit: Selective Edge--Server Map Acquisition for Cross-User Travel-Mode Recognition
comments: 5 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: Networked mobility sensing couples local trajectory inference with remote geospatial context, making communication decisions part of the prediction system. We present GeoSplit, an edge--server framework for travel-mode recognition that separates the utility of map evidence, its training-time transfer, and its selective acquisition at runtime. On GeoLife with 10% labels, we evaluate these components under user-day and user-disjoint grouping. For unseen users, aligned full-map context raises macro-F1 from 0.7154 to 0.7864, while map-informed distillation yields a motion-only student at 0.7225. Through a compact query interface, entropy gating achieves 0.7729 macro-F1 versus 0.7738 for all queries, querying 39.5% of trajectories and reducing application payload by 60.5%. Under user-day grouping, selective and all-query scores are similarly close at a 21.6% query rate. Learned value estimation and probability fusion offer no consistent improvement. These results illustrate communication-efficient edge--server inference for an intelligent transportation sensing task.

title: Doubly Robust Learning of Heterogeneous Survival Treatment Effects under Time-Varying Treatments
abstract: Estimating heterogeneous survival treatment effects (HSTEs) from time-to-event data under time-varying treatments is important in fields such as medicine (e.g., to decide which sequence of treatments is better in terms of survival probability). However, this task is challenging because treatment decisions, patient characteristics, and censoring probability often evolve together, requiring sequential adjustment for both treatments and censoring. Existing survival learners mostly consider a single baseline treatment assignment, while longitudinal treatment-effect learners typically assume uncensored outcomes. In this paper, we introduce a novel doubly robust learner for heterogeneous survival treatment effects under time-varying treatments and history-dependent censoring. Our framework separates the intervention window from the survival horizon, with treatment prescribed for a finite period, after which care follows its natural course. We further establish the favorable theoretical properties of Neyman-orthogonality, rate double robustness and quasi-oracle efficiency. The framework accommodates flexible machine learning models for nuisance estimation and treatment-effect regression. We evaluate our learners through several numerical experiments, demonstrating their effectiveness.

title: Deep Pontryagin Learning for Continuous-Time Stochastic Control with Jumps
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
abstract: We develop a deep Pontryagin learning framework for high-dimensional continuous-time stochastic control problems that naturally accommodates jump-diffusions. In contrast to direct policy optimization, which repeatedly differentiates the objective through the entire time-discretized dynamics, our method separates adjoint learning from policy improvement by explicitly incorporating state-sensitivity information from the Pontryagin stochastic maximum principle. For a fixed Markov control, we first compute pathwise adjoint labels by backpropagating the reward through time along simulated state trajectories, and project these labels onto the Markov state through a supervised regression step. The control is then updated by enforcing the pointwise Hamiltonian stationarity condition. We prove that the resulting projected adjoint process satisfies a discrete-time Pontryagin principle and converges, as the time step tends to zero, to the solution of the corresponding continuous-time adjoint backward stochastic differential equation. Numerical experiments illustrate the accuracy, stability, and scalability of the approach.

title: Copying Under Repetition: From Prefix Matching to Position Hashing
abstract: Frontier LLMs can copy random text almost flawlessly, yet they often overrun or truncate long blocks of repeated characters. In repeated strings, matching local content no longer reliably identifies where copying should continue or when it should stop. Nevertheless, we show that a two-layer transformer with $O(\log\log N)$-bit precision and $O(\log N/\log\log N)$ width can copy every string up to a chosen design horizon $N$ and terminate correctly under arbitrary repetition. We use RoPE-style rotations of attention values and outputs (VO-rotations) with small prime periods to encode distances from delimiter anchors modulo those primes. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, these periodic encodings jointly distinguish all required distances, allowing one retrieval rule to select either the next source token or the end marker. In contrast, we prove a width-independent impossibility result for copying under sequential finite-precision softmax accumulation. It applies to transformers whose only positional input is an additive attention bias that eventually becomes constant, including NoPE and a recursive implementation of ALiBi. Once an identical-token run exceeds the resulting saturation threshold, further repetitions leave the logits unchanged. If this threshold grows sublinearly with $N$, these models cannot both complete a long all-identical copy and stop correctly, a pattern resembling the termination errors of frontier LLMs. In synthetic copying experiments, baseline transformer models fail on long repeated strings even within the training range. Trained VO models, by contrast, generalize beyond the training lengths with near-perfect accuracy up to length $\approx 5005$, the selected primes' period product.

title: Cross-Fitting for Neural Posterior Estimation
comments: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026
abstract: Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) fits an amortized conditional density estimator to a simulated training set of complete-data realizations. NPE's training objective, log-likelihood, favors posterior approximations that assign arbitrarily high density to the training points, and typical families of amortized conditional density estimators (e.g., normalizing flows, Gaussian encoders) are flexible enough to oblige. The resulting policy of extreme overconfidence translates poorly to held-out data. Early stopping and other regularizers can prevent this degeneracy, but they are limited to selecting posterior approximations along an unfavorable optimization trajectory set by in-sample residuals, where the posterior mean is underfit while the posterior variance is overfit. To avoid this trade-off, we propose Cross-Fitting NPE (CF-NPE), which uses sample splitting to separate conditional-mean estimation from the estimation of the posterior's higher moments. Using $K$-fold cross-fitting, CF-NPE fits $K$ posterior-mean regressors and then fits a conditional density estimator to the resulting out-of-fold residuals. In experiments with synthetic data and in a cosmological application, CF-NPE achieves higher held-out log-likelihood than standard NPE and typically improves calibration. CF-NPE is most useful in high-dimensional, simulation-limited settings.

title: recAMPLIFY: Large-Scale Pretraining of Recursive Protein Language Models
comments: Models: this https URL Code: this https URL
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL)
abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) are powerful tools for protein annotation and mutation-effect prediction, but progress has largely depended on scaling model size and data, making them expensive and prone to memorization. Test-time scaling offers a complementary path, but methods developed for autoregressive LLMs do not transfer directly: masked encoders lack a generation loop, and amino acids do not verbalize in a reasoning language. Instead, we adapt recursive pretraining to masked pLMs, where a weight-tied Transformer core refines residue-aligned hidden states over an adjustable number of cycles. We instantiate this recipe as recAMPLIFY, a pLM with 155M unique parameters trained on the same 2T tokens as AMPLIFY-350M. Despite 56% fewer parameters, it improves CASP contact recovery and three out of four supervised tasks, notably raising fold accuracy by 22.5%. Because optimal depth for recAMPLIFY varies across tasks and assays, we then introduce Gated Mixture Recurrence (GMR), a framework that decodes each protein from a probability-weighted mixture of hidden states visited during recursion. GMR employs a learned residual gate at scalar, low-rank, or per-dimension resolution to control how much of each cycle's proposed update is accepted into the state. This unifies halting and gating into a single adaptive computation objective while recovering PonderNet-style halting as a special case without gates. Layered on top of recAMPLIFY, GMR further reduces expected layer depth by up to 37%, although the accuracy trade-off varies by task. Mechanistic analyses show that residual gating controls recurrence stability beyond the trained depth and that halt depth tracks biological properties.

title: Trajectory Replay: Continuous-Time Mixture Transport for Lifelong Generative Models
abstract: Adapting pre-trained continuous-time generative models to sequentially incoming data without forgetting earlier tasks is a central challenge in lifelong learning. A leading strategy, generative replay, uses a generative model trained on historical tasks to augment its own continual update with synthetic samples from experience. However, it requires full trajectory simulations at every training step, which accumulate discretization errors and can degrade the replayed historical distribution. Here, we propose trajectory replay, which bypasses sample generation by training an updated velocity field to match both a frozen historical velocity along its trajectories and the incoming task's velocity field, weighted by a stability-plasticity coefficient. Through the lens of continuous-time transport, we show the resulting optimum averages the two task velocities by their respective densities and generates the mixture of their probability paths. Combined with mean velocity distillation, trajectory replay accesses historical trajectories using only a few network evaluations per continual update. Empirically, it outperforms generative replay and distillation baselines on class-incremental image generation. In two biological case studies, trajectory replay extends generative perturbation models to new contexts and experimental batches across two data modalities while preserving treatment-effect prediction.

title: Simulation Priors for Rapid Adaptation in Model-Based RL for Autonomous Racing
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: Reinforcement learning enables learning high-performance control policies, but its reliance on extensive interaction limits deployment on physical systems where data collection is costly, and failures are unsafe. We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based RL framework that uses structured simulation priors for rapid adaptation. PIA pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories, then adapts it with limited target-domain interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning. Rather than requiring an accurate simulator for policy transfer, PIA treats simulated trajectories as biased priors whose residual mismatch is corrected during online adaptation. We evaluate PIA in autonomous racing using high-fidelity simulation and on a real full-size autonomous race car. In simulation, PIA adapts faster across track and surface shifts than strong baselines, achieving lower lap times and fewer failures. On hardware, PIA achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.

title: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs
comments: 41 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables, under review
abstract: Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents. Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs. We introduce HarnessPro, a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost. In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses. Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses normalized weighted squared-distance selection to provide cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) harnesses for different deployment budgets. Selected harnesses enter the next iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates. Our experiments cover Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench, using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Across these benchmarks using GPT-5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves an average pass-rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an average per-task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO. This advantage also holds when using GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at this https URL

title: Topological Sheaves of Irreducibility: A Theoretical Framework for Multi-Agent Task Obstructions
comments: 31 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables
abstract: Multi-agent systems can differ under identical agents and communication budgets when they support different forms of joint interaction. We introduce Topological Sheaves of Irreducibility (TSI), a sheaf-theoretic framework separating task-level compatibility obstructions from system capability. A task is represented by an interaction complex $K$ and a capacity sheaf $\mathcal{F}$; nonzero $H^n(K;\mathcal{F})$ defines a structural signature, while registered interventions test capability. For cocycle data, cochain realization is solvable exactly when the represented cohomology class vanishes. Examples show that the signature is sheaf-relative, and the degree-1 reduction yields cycle-space witnesses and observation requirements. We evaluate two finite one-round models. Across 15,625 degree-1 inputs, an all-agent additive primitive solves decision and repair exactly; the optimal pairwise system reaches 88.80% on decision, one input above the 88.79% majority-class baseline, and 26.63% on repair. On a degree-2 tetrahedral-boundary task over 531,441 inputs, the same-2-skeleton system retains all four three-agent primitives yet matches the pairwise-only optimum throughout the registered separation window, whereas adding the class-filling four-agent primitive makes both tasks exact. Status-preserving robustness checks retain exact performance but are not cost-matched to the class-restoring ablation. Conditional on the registered primitives and cost models, TSI provides task-relative, falsifiable tests of higher-order interaction.

title: Training with ML-labeled Data via Stochastic First- and Zeroth-Order Optimization
abstract: Training a machine learning (ML) model is an optimization process that typically requires a set of examples with ground-truth labels beforehand. Obtaining these ground truths usually requires laborious human effort and can be costly. The scalability of human labeling becomes a concern when there are a large number of data points that need to be labeled. To address this practical issue, we consider an optimization setting where a subset of samples has ground-truth labels, while the remaining data points were labeled by an ML predictor, which could potentially assign incorrect labels to those points. We propose both first-order and zeroth-order stochastic optimization methods for training on datasets consisting of a mix of true-labeled and ML-labeled samples. We further conduct comprehensive empirical studies from training a linear regression model to fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) to showcase the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms for training with ML-labeled data.

title: On Data Scaling in Tabular ML: More Data, Better Generalization?
comments: Code at: this https URL
abstract: Recent work in tabular machine learning has emphasized the importance of diverse and realistic evaluation settings. The niche of large-scale (1M+) data, however, remains under-explored. To study training-data scaling, we assemble eight real-world tabular datasets with up to around ten million training examples, retaining the natural distribution shifts of the tasks and using random-split evaluation as a control. We find that GBDTs and MLP-based models show broadly similar scaling trends, with gains from both additional training data and algorithmic improvements. Tabular foundation models show more varied scaling behavior, with recent versions benefiting more consistently from larger contexts even under distribution shift. However, scaling training data under distribution shift introduces new challenges: in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance mostly improve together at smaller scales but can diverge at larger scales. We examine this through MLP capacity sweeps and comparisons of the validation distributions used for tuning and early stopping in MLPs and GBDTs. We also compare common practices of using validation data, contrasting its use for model selection in MLP pipelines with using it for in-context fitting in tabular foundation model pipelines. Under stronger shifts, MLPs selected using validation representative of the evaluation conditions generally maintain or improve performance as training data grows. In contrast, including such examples in context improves foundation-model performance, but does not prevent deterioration with increasing training size in our experiments.

title: Two hidden layer suffice: the caterpillar net
comments: 17 pages. Lean formalization and paper sources: this https URL
abstract: Every continuous piecewise linear (CPWL) function is a finite signed sum of maxima of affine functions, making maximum representation a central problem in the study of the expressiveness of ReLU networks. A now-disproved conjecture predicted logarithmic depth for maxima. Inspired by the proof by Brunck et al. (2026) that two hidden layers suffice for general CPWL functions, we give the Caterpillar Net, a nonrecursive construction for the maximum of $N$ inputs with two hidden layers of widths $O(N^2)$ and $2^{O(N\log N)}$. The construction has a direct geometric interpretation.

title: Learning to Refer: Inference-Time Collaboration in Decentralized Federated Learning
abstract: In decentralized federated learning, heterogeneous clients may develop complementary expertise, yet each query is typically evaluated only by the client where it arrives. To exploit this distributed expertise without global coordination, we formulate inference-time collaboration as budgeted local expert referral, a graph-constrained routing process in which a query can move only between neighboring clients and only visited clients contribute to its final prediction. EdgeDRM implements this framework by learning a density-based routing potential for each client: differences between neighboring potentials provide the comparisons used to select successive referrals, while local task models generate predictions that are aggregated along the resulting route. Both training and inference are decentralized, using only neighbor-local information without a central router or graph-wide client scoring. We establish estimation guarantees for the learned comparisons and characterize how local improvement and graph structure govern prior-weighted density gains from referral. Experiments on benchmark and real-world medical data show that EdgeDRM outperforms graph-matched decentralized baselines in most settings, with the clearest benefits under sparse connectivity.

title: Scaling Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Brain Encoding
comments: 38 pages, 13 figures, 20 tables. Code available at this https URL
abstract: Brain encoding models aim to predict neural responses to stimuli. The most widely used approach fits readouts from frozen pretrained backbones. Using neural data to train large models from scratch or fully fine-tune them after task-pretraining has proven difficult because neural data is costly and limited. We show that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables us to effectively adapt very large pretrained backbones for brain encoding with a small number of trainable parameters. To make it computationally practical, we exploit the backbone's causal structure to predict multiple timepoints in a single pass instead of using sliding windows, significantly reducing feature-extraction cost. This enables efficient fine-tuning of multimodal backbones with up to 104B parameters, the largest model adapted for brain encoding to our knowledge. Trained with a low-rank adapter (LoRA) and a lightweight readout, our approach consistently improves brain encoding performance across nine diverse multimodal backbones. On the same Qwen3-Omni backbone as the prior state-of-the-art (SoTA), our method BrainLoRA achieves the best published performance on the Algonauts 2025 Challenge. We also show the adapted multimodal backbones remain interpretable: modality attribution recovers the canonical sensory topography that prior work often obtains by construction from separate unimodal encoders, and neural adaptation increases the contribution of audio inputs and cross-modal mixing within the backbone. To scale out the number of adapted models, we develop a multi-LoRA kernel that accelerates joint training of multiple LoRAs on a shared backbone. This enables an ensemble of 200+ adapted models that ranks first on the public Algonauts post-challenge leaderboard at the time of writing. Together, our results highlight PEFT as an efficient and powerful paradigm for brain encoding.

title: Next Best Action: Causal Constrained Offline RL for Business Action Targeting
comments: Accepted for oral presentation at the ACM RecSys 2026 Workshop on Online and Adaptive Recommender System (OARS)
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Information Retrieval (cs.IR); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
abstract: Next Best Action (NBA) systems must select among customer interventions (e.g., discounts, promotions, and lifecycle actions), maximize long-term economic value, satisfy complex operational constraints, and remain causally grounded. Existing approaches lack a rigorous framework for meeting these requirements jointly. We address this gap by formulating NBA as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP). We then integrate off-policy causal correction of the estimated customer dynamics directly into the Linear Programming (LP) formulation of the CMDP. The resulting policy selects actions based on customer states to maximize long-term value while explicitly enforcing business guardrails. Furthermore, the LP formulation yields shadow prices that quantify the economic trade-offs of operational constraints (e.g., fairness and user welfare), enhancing policy interpretability. We validate our proposed offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework on an industry case study involving rideshare coupon targeting, where customer states are defined by Recency, Frequency, and Monetary (RFM) stages. We evaluate performance using model-based off-policy evaluation, with causal dynamics estimated from a temporal holdout. Under the observed coupon budget and RFM state representation, our optimized policy improves customer lifetime value (LTV) by 19% over the estimated behavior policy and 8% over a myopic baseline. Although the demonstrated action space is binary, the proposed framework is action-agnostic, yielding a general-purpose decision module for targeting systems that manage multiple interventions.

title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
abstract: We propose KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a novel update rule for associative matrix memories. KronLSTM extends the xLSTM family with a memory-revision mechanism that corrects targeted associations while modifying the memory only along a single direction in matrix space. This minimally invasive memory revision reduces interference with previously stored information compared with delta-rule updates, making it particularly well suited for long-context language modeling. The resulting memory dynamics can be mathematically described as a Markov chain that converges to a steady-state distribution, while the expected norm of the memory matrix remains uniformly bounded throughout the entire input sequence. Hence, KronLSTM ensures stable memory dynamics without requiring additional normalization and stabilization mechanisms for the memory state. Experiments show that KronLSTM is competitive with, and often outperforms, existing linear attention architectures, including models of the (Gated) DeltaNet family, with particularly strong performance on long context benchmarks. These results establish the Kronecker Delta Rule as an effective and analytically tractable foundation for stable associative memory in recurrent linear attention architectures. Our code (this https URL) and models (this https URL) are open-source.

title: Text-to-Image Generative Modeling Without Language Pretraining
comments: 27 pages; Project website: this https URL
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Modern text-to-image (T2I) systems use internet-scale language pretraining for text-conditioned image generation. We ask whether language pretraining is necessary for strong T2I generation. We introduce Halcyon, a family of early-fusion multimodal autoregressive models pretrained entirely from scratch on GPIC, a dataset of 100M image-text pairs. Halcyon-0.52B outperforms LlamaGen-XL/8 (48.0 vs. 63.3 gFD) with 18.2$\times$ less pretraining compute. Further, Halcyon-1.6B outperforms JiT-T2I-XXL/8++ (35.3 vs. 41.0 gFD) with 275$\times$ less pretraining compute. Controlled experiments show that text-only pretraining does not improve T2I generation. Halcyon also learns image captioning by replacing caption dropout with I2T supervision, maintaining competitive T2I generation quality under the same pretraining budget. We show that strong T2I systems can be trained from scratch without internet-scale language pretraining. Code and models are available at this https URL

title: Anytime Contracts for AI Services
comments: 19 pages, 3 figures
subjects: Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: AI services are prone to moral hazard, as model providers can silently route requests to cheaper, lower-quality models, and the inherent stochasticity of model outputs makes this degradation hard to detect. Contract theory addresses moral hazard by designing payment rules that reward high-quality outputs and prevent strategic overcharging. However, existing frameworks assume interactions of fixed duration, whereas AI services are typically consumed through subscriptions and pay-as-you-go APIs that users can terminate at any time based on observed performance. We show that this flexibility can break standard contracts, opening them up to abuse by either the providers or users. To address this, we extend contract theory to account for unknown exit rules. We formalize the problem as a Principal-Agent game, and show that budget-optimal contracts in this setting are proportional to anytime-valid hypothesis tests based on likelihood-ratio e-values. We give an efficient algorithm for computing anytime contracts and show how betting e-processes can be used to approximate them when the models are unknown. Finally, we evaluate our findings on synthetic data and data from deployed LLMs.

title: Measuring the Influence of Modality-Specific Node Representations on Graphs
subjects: Social and Information Networks (cs.SI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Multimedia (cs.MM)
abstract: Multimodal attributed graphs combine graph structure with node text and image representations in recommendation and multimedia analysis. Graph predictors propagate these representations across connected nodes, so one input can change predictions at its own and nearby nodes. Measuring this distributed response reveals which modality-specific inputs a trained model relies on and how predictor design changes that reliance. We study influence measurement for modality-specific node representations. Given an encoded graph, a trained predictor, a training split, and fixed candidate representations, the task outputs one influence score per candidate and separate text and image rankings. We score a candidate by replacing it with its modality's training-node mean and comparing the original and changed predictions. Existing feature attribution and data valuation generally target one output, training examples, whole nodes, or graph elements rather than prediction changes across graph nodes. Our empirical study shows that nearby-node responses contain information missed by source-only scores and simple proxies, while response magnitude alone does not identify which class changes support the task. Guided by these observations, we propose MoGI (Modality-specific Graph Influence). It propagates training labels to define task direction, reads the same replacement response for the favored class and full class distribution, and averages the resulting ranks. MoGI requires no predictor retraining or learned scoring parameters. Under a shared five-dataset, eight-predictor benchmark, it achieves the largest aggregate held-out loss increase against all five external methods at every tested ranking cutoff.

title: DUET: Decoupled Upper- and Lower-Body Execution for Task-Agnostic Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
abstract: Changing a humanoid robot's manipulation policy should not require retraining the controller that maintains the robot's balance. This study introduces DUET, a decoupled execution framework that enables locomotion and manipulation controllers to operate simultaneously by combining their commands only at the robot interface. A reinforcement-learning locomotion policy controls the 12 leg joints and a waist yaw joint, tracking planar velocity, turning rate, and pelvis height from deep crouching to upright standing on a 23-degree-of-freedom Unitree G1. The 10 arm joints are excluded from the action space, while their positions and velocities are included only as observations, so that any compatible manipulation policy that generates arm-joint targets can control the upper body, and the locomotion policy keeps the lower body stable without requiring shared training or direct coordination. This study demonstrates the modular approach on hardware by pairing the same locomotion checkpoint with two different vision-language-action models, GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5. In simulation evaluation, the locomotion controller kept the robot's lower body stable with no falls while tracking the commanded planar velocity, yaw rate, and pelvis height with errors of 0.186 m/s, 0.142 rad/s, and 0.016 m, respectively. Ablation studies identify the upper-body pose curriculum as the dominant component, and removing this training step reduces episode survival from 20.0 to 7.4 seconds and increases the fall rate to 6.06 per environment minute. Robustness tests show no falls under pushes of up to 1.0 m/s within the trained payload range, and no falls at twice the payload limit for pushes below 0.7 m/s. These results show that a manipulation policy can be exchanged without retraining, restarting, or otherwise touching the layer that keeps the robot upright.

title: Language-Forcing: Advancing Humanoid Loco-Manipulation via Semantic Alignment of Whole-Body World Action Models
comments: 9 pages of main text, 31 pages of appendix
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict robot actions and future observations. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly distinguish task-relevant transitions from incidental scene changes. For whole-body policies, this distinction matters because task progress depends on coordinated changes in body pose, contact, and object state. We introduce LANGUAGE-FORCING, a training strategy that uses language to emphasize task-relevant changes in the future visual representations of a whole-body WAM. Given paired current and ground- truth short-horizon future frames, a frozen vision-language model assesses task progress and predicts plausible subsequent state changes. We encode these descriptions with a frozen text encoder and align their embeddings with intermediate, action-conditioned future-visual features, complementing the original visual and action prediction objectives. All auxiliary components are used only during training, introducing no additional inference overhead. On HumanoidArena, LANGUAGE-FORCING achieves an average success rate of 79.17%, exceeding the strongest competing policy by 9.46 percentage points and the same WAM without language alignment by 10.77 percentage points. Across five real-world tasks, language alignment raises average success from 53.33% to 71.33% over the same WAM baseline.

title: EAGLE: Entropy-Aware Geometric Learning Enhancer for Partially Polygon-Supervised Object Localization
comments: 25 Pages, 3 figures, submitted to International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) 2027
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Object detection is a critical application of computer vision, yet models trained uniformly on bounding boxes lack the geometric precision to be fully effective in inference settings, especially at high IoU thresholds. One common approach is the introduction of polygon-supervised localization, where a model is trained explicitly for localization but with access to polygon masks during training. Among such methods, partial polygon supervision is viable due to the higher annotation costs of developing fully supervised training datasets. However, this introduces a further challenge: in object classes of relatively low shape complexity, the addition of training masks and subsequent segmentation loss may obscure box localization, often worsening model performance despite access to deeper geometric information. To address the practical limitations of both full and partial polygon supervision, we introduce a mathematical framework for quantifying per-class geometric complexity by combining information theory and statistical shape analysis. With this framework, we develop Entropy-Aware Geometric Learning Enhancer (EAGLE), a lightweight, post-training model head that learns geometric information for the localization model, improving accuracy via edge refinement and localization rescoring using entropy-informed updates. Empirical analysis across MS COCO and Pascal SBD demonstrates the entropy framework meaningfully predicts shape reconstruction error and accuracy differences among mask-derived and standard box predictions, while the implemented EAGLE framework achieves consistent improvement on already SOTA detection frameworks (+0.9 mAP50-95 points on MS COCO) at minimal observed inference overhead.

title: Your Self-Supervised Projection Head Captures Object Co-Occurrence Statistics
comments: Accepted for publication in NeuRIPS
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) has achieved impressive success in learning semantic visual representations, yet the underlying principles driving this success remain underexplored. In this work, we hypothesize that common SSL pretext tasks implicitly model object co-occurrence statistics, a fundamental cue for visual learning. To test this, we curate three datasets of segmented objects from existing vision benchmarks using a state-of-the-art segmentation model. Through experiments across many SSL models, we reveal a hierarchical encoding of semantic information: while the visual backbone captures object categories, the projection head specializes in encoding co-occurrences between object categories. As a result, the projection head outperforms the backbone in aligning with human judgments of inter-category similarity. Furthermore, by controlling co-occurrence patterns during pre-training, we demonstrate that encoding object co-occurrences can significantly accelerate the emergence of category-level representations. Our findings uncover a previously hidden learning principle in SSL and suggest a path toward designing more effective pretext tasks by explicitly leveraging object co-occurrence structure.

title: VERDICT: Visual Extraction-Result Decoder with Integrated Confidence and Traceable Evidence
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Workshop on VLM4RWD
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Enterprises run schema-guided structured field extraction on documents with frontier multimodal models, and accuracy keeps improving as new models and systems arrive. Two things have not kept pace: the evidence for each extracted value, meaning the location of the document it was read from, and how far to trust the value and that evidence. Neither is a component of most extraction systems today, so we build them as a framework that attaches to an existing extractor and leaves it untouched. We present VERDICT, a plug-in framework that uses a small Vision--Language Model (VLM) to ground/localize the evidence once per document over a fixed external extractor's output, then calibrates value and evidence confidence. Fine-tuning the VLM for evidence localization substantially improves visual evidence quality and, more importantly, expands VERDICT's selective-prediction operating range. At a strict confidence threshold $0.80$, VERDICT with the fine-tuned VLM gives usable precision--coverage trade-offs for both value and evidence confidence across the in-distribution and out of distribution datasets, whereas the frozen setting often collapses to little or no coverage. Running an open-weight VLM for localization rather than a closed API makes its internal states available to the calibrator, and they are worth more than output log-probabilities: in-distribution AUROC rises from $0.730$ to $0.914$ for value confidence and from $0.681$ to $0.906$ for evidence confidence. This advantage does not survive a distribution shift. We show that the signal is displaced rather than destroyed, and that labeling roughly $120$ fields from the target dataset takes evidence confidence from $0.641$ to $0.905$ on one dataset and from $0.675$ to $0.829$ on the other.

title: A Controlled LLM Workflow for Evidence-Grounded Diagnosis of Risk Score Differences
comments: Accepted for presentation at the International Conference on Electrical and Computer Engineering Researches (ICECER 2026), December 3-5, 2026
abstract: We propose a controlled Large Language Model (LLM) workflow for explaining risk score differences using similar historical transactions. The workflow combines reference retrieval and contrastive SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) evidence with reference-based LLM reasoning and deterministic validation. Experiments on a test dataset show that the workflow produces more consistent, evidence-grounded and traceable diagnoses than the same LLM without structured workflow guidance.

title: IMPULSE: Push First, Then Predict in V-JEPA 2 Feature Space
comments: 8 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Latent world models such as V-JEPA 2 forecast in the feature space of a video encoder, but one look at an object does not reveal how hard it is to rotate, how much it bounces or how much it slides. People find out by trying: a few pokes reveal how an object responds. IMPULSE, named after the impulse response it infers, gives a predictor in frozen V-JEPA 2 feature space the same ability. A Bayesian contact memory summarizes three short calibration pushes, a predicted object pose carries it into the predictor, and a lightweight random-Fourier pose head lets the predictor use the pose. On 512 fresh objects, in a pre-specified held-out confirmation with models sealed before the data existed, the memory lowers the 1-second feature-forecast error by 11.6-12.8% relative to the same predictor without experience, for all 8 training seeds, with a 95% seed-and-object interval excluding zero.
