The gain also holds for 128 objects with out-of-range physics (11.7-14.0%), and the full extension beats a plain predictor by 15.5-16.6%. An information-ladder argument, exact for ideal predictors, shows that physics reaches the features only through motion, so we measure how much the pathway lets pose help. On fresh objects, the Fourier head roughly triples the gain of a perfect memory over plain pose tokens (2.8-3.2x). Raw push measurements fed through the same pathway give a similar gain, so the Bayesian summary is not required; it condenses the trials into eight interpretable numbers. The gain is absent at contact onset and grows afterwards.

title: Super-resolution as Spatial Downscaling: Coherence, Structure and Task Utility in Earth Observation
comments: 41 pages, 12 figures. Code: this https URL
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Learned satellite super-resolution is commonly assessed by pixel fidelity and potential downlink savings, but these criteria do not establish whether the reconstructed field preserves spatial structure or supports reliable downstream analysis. We treat single-image super-resolution as a spatial downscaling problem and evaluate four lightweight networks, including our compact 0.36 million-parameter model, against interpolation using pixel metrics, directional variograms, spectral band correlation, codispersion and observation coherence. On 735 satellite tiles from 190 scenes, the networks differ by at most 0.03dB and outperform bicubic interpolation by $1.39-1.42$dB at $\times 2$. They recover about 30% of the spectral power above the observation's Nyquist frequency and, at $\times 4$, produce more isotropic fields than the reference (range anisotropy 0.59 against 0.49). Energy-based metrics can favour invented detail. Enforcing coherence reaches the quantisation limit, yet at least 99.7% of the remaining error lies in the observation operator's null space, which coherence cannot constrain. Under spatially blocked, paired evaluation with two backbones and a sharpening control, learned reconstruction changes land-use accuracy by $-1.0$ to $+3.1$ percentage points (significant in 7 of 24 comparisons) and building-change F1 by $-0.015$ to $+0.024$ (none significant) relative to bicubic interpolation, and amplifies spurious change between two observations of an unchanged scene by $1.3-1.5$ times where interpolation attenuates it. Full-resolution JPEG\,2000 matches or exceeds reduced-resolution transmission with reconstruction at every matched bitrate. Learned reconstruction is most useful when only low-resolution imagery is available, and its evaluation should combine pixel metrics with spatial structure, observation coherence and task-level tests under spatial validation.

title: LLM Evolutionary Search Strategies Should be Compared by Tokens
subjects: Neural and Evolutionary Computing (cs.NE); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: LLM evolutionary search is currently evaluated by counting proposals (candidate programs). We demonstrate this metric hides the true cost of search, and redo the comparison using tokens. By replaying 600 logged runs across 5 tasks and 3 methods, we show that proposal costs vary wildly from 16k to 39k tokens. In equal-proposal comparisons, this silently grants some methods up to 1.9x the compute of others, and gives evolution roughly 6x the budget of independent sampling. When we match token budgets, giving sampling six times more attempts, and remove scorer exploits, the evolutionary advantage largely vanishes. Evolution beats independent sampling by 5% or less on 12 of 15 task-method pairs, retaining a 23 to 28% margin on only 3, all on one task. A replication with Claude Haiku 4.5 reproduces this split, though a third backbone shows its size depends on the model too. The performance margin justifying these systems is often an accounting artifact. Reporting tokens, not proposals and not model calls, fixes this and costs nothing, as the logs already hold them.

title: Weakly Supervised Discovery of Motion Styles for Compositional Robot Control
abstract: When a robot possesses more degrees of freedom than a task requires, multiple trajectories can achieve the same objective using distinct motion styles. Compositional robot control aims to preserve a selected style while simultaneously executing an independent task command, effectively balancing these potentially competing objectives. In this paper, we present CODES, a framework for compositional robot control that discovers a coherent style repertoire from diverse recordings and composes it with independent commands. First, motion retargeting maps the recordings to motions executable by the target robot; next, weakly supervised consensus encoding and density-based clustering identify styles within and across recordings without a prescribed count; finally, reinforcement learning trains a policy to compose the discovered styles with independent commands. We evaluate CODES on a Unitree Go2 quadruped across two simulators and physical hardware. Compared to baselines, CODES significantly improves kinematic coherence. Furthermore, our controller successfully tracks velocity commands that generalize beyond the support of the recorded data, exhibiting robust and distinguishable style characteristics during both cross-simulator and real-world hardware deployments. Project website: this https URL

title: Unified Multiparadigm Fusion Intelligence for Rare Disease Diagnosis
comments: 26 pages, 5 figures
abstract: Rare diseases (RDs) affect an estimated 300 million people globally, leaving patients to navigate a protracted diagnostic odyssey constrained by clinical scarcity and fragmented medical knowledge. Artificial intelligence (AI) has progressively advanced RD diagnostics, from symbolic methods and deep learning to large language model (LLM)-based systems. However, each paradigm carries structural limitations: symbolic methods are bounded by knowledge completeness, neural models sacrifice interpretability, and LLM-based systems are vulnerable to evaluation biases like data leakage. In this study, we introduce FusionRare, a unified multiparadigm fusion framework integrating knowledge-driven symbolic reasoning, deep-learning pattern recognition, case-based patient retrieval, and LLM-based heuristic inference via statistical meta-aggregation and knowledge-enhanced agentic reflection. Evaluated on 2,528 strictly isolated clinical cases, FusionRare achieves state-of-the-art RD prioritization, attaining a macro-averaged Recall @1 of 51% for phenotype-only diagnosis and 79% for phenotype-genotype joint analysis. These results represent decisive advantages over the advanced agentic system DeepRare, frontier LLMs including GPT 5.5, and specialized tools like PhenoBrain and LIRICAL under stringent anti-leakage protocols. A randomized, crossover clinician-AI validation demonstrated that FusionRare elevates the true diagnostic rank in 45% of decisions, improves physician confidence in 62%, and reduces time to diagnosis by 21%. These findings indicate that reconciling these orthogonal AI paradigms significantly enhances diagnostic capabilities, bridging the gap between computational benchmarks and actionable clinical reliability. More broadly, this work provides a replicable framework for deploying trustworthy diagnostic AI across complex, high-stakes, and underserved medical domains.

title: When Does Evidence-Graph Structure Predict Answer Correctness? Label-Free Abstention for Structured Retrieval
comments: 34 pages, 5 figures, 37 tables. Under review at ACM Transactions on Information Systems
abstract: Retrieval systems return scored answers, but a high score does not show that an answer should be trusted. The proposed training-free abstention method applies the boundary cut to the selected evidence in an evidence graph. The signal is the weighted cut between selected and unselected candidates and requires no correctness labels or confidence-model training. On MemoryAgentBench (MAB) FactConsolidation multi-hop, with unresolved queries ranked last for every selector, it raises area under the precision-coverage curve from 0.736 for the best score baseline to 0.785 (+0.049, 95% CI [+0.008, +0.092]); under the native evaluation, where score baselines keep their unresolved values, the gap is +0.108. A zero-cut subset contains 71 of 400 queries at 100% observed precision. In this pipeline, the subset corresponds to structural closure; controlled analyses attribute much of the remaining separation to resolution status, with little benefit from continuous edge weights. Across external benchmarks, usefulness varies with graph construction, edge semantics, and relation; typed structure alone does not ensure useful confidence. A supervised gradient-boosted selector achieves 0.814 versus the boundary cut's 0.785 when the retrieval stack matches. These findings provide empirical guidance for using available evidence graphs for lightweight, auditable post-retrieval abstention without additional model inference.

title: ToolRosetta: Surface-Form Invariance of Tool-Call Guards
comments: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (AIWILD). 4 pages plus appendices
abstract: Step-level guards for tool-using agents are evaluated on tidy JSON tool calls, but deployed coding agents act through execute_bash and execute_code tools whose payloads are strings. We introduce ToolRosetta, which re-renders every candidate action in the AgentDojo and AgentHarm splits of TS-Bench as a Python call, as a shell command, and without the agent's rationale. The renderings are produced by code and verified by round-trip parsing, so the user request, the history, the label and the action's effect stay fixed while only the surface form changes. Across eleven guards with two placebo controls, frontier and strong open-weight guards are stable: no frontier error rate moves by more than 3.4 points. Four of five specialized agent guards are not: under the shell form their false-positive rates rise by 21 to 47 points on AgentDojo, and TS-Guard's by 38 points on its own home benchmark, blocking between a third and nine in ten benign actions; the fifth, StepGuard, does not move. A small open guard drifts five points more permissive. Removing the agent's rationale moves most guards whose input carries it, in guard-specific directions. A request-blind control on one guard shows that the rationale is where intent is read from. A parser that restores the canonical call in front of the guard removes the effect for these renderings, by construction. Benchmark accuracy on JSON calls does not predict a guard's operating point behind a code-acting agent.

title: Location, Location, Generation: Where You Ask Matters for Generative Engine Optimization
comments: 4 pages
subjects: Information Retrieval (cs.IR); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Social and Information Networks (cs.SI)
abstract: Generative search engines answer local and commercial questions with a written answer and a few cited sources. A growing practice of generative engine optimization (GEO) monitors which sources and brands these answers show, typically from a single place. In this paper, we present a controlled audit of how the user's location changes the sources that generative engines cite. We ask 300 questions of ChatGPT with 19 declared locations, and of ChatGPT and Gemini from five network locations, each twice to measure run-to-run noise (31,200 answers). The engines take location from different channels. ChatGPT follows the location an application declares, down to the city: it writes the place into its own searches, and its search backend localizes results even when the queries name no place. It ignores the network. Gemini ignores the declared location and follows the country of the network, changing most of its sources even for questions that do not depend on place. The businesses the answers recommend change with the sources. Thus, visibility in generative search is specific to the user's location, and audits must control both channels.

title: Interpretability of AI weather models via intermediate decoding
comments: 16 pages, 10 figures, 1 table. Supplementary material in the ancillary files
subjects: Atmospheric and Oceanic Physics (physics.ao-ph); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: AI weather prediction models are often regarded as black boxes. Despite their impressive skill, there is little understanding of how the input data is processed during inference to produce the forecast. This limitation arises from the use of high-dimensional latent representations in which individual dimensions are no longer directly interpretable in physical terms. To gain insight into how forecasts are constructed, we propose the method of intermediate decoding for AI weather models and apply it to GraphCast, Aurora and ArchesWeather. In this approach, latent states from intermediate depths are decoded back into meteorological fields. To do this, we use the decoder that has been trained to output the forecast at the end of processing. Since latent states at different depths do not share a consistent basis, we train affine transformations that align intermediate latent states with the decoder's expected input space. Applying this framework to the three models yields the following results. First, the skill of forecasts at intermediate stages of processing improves gradually through the processor layers. Second, bypassing all processor blocks shows that the encoder-decoder pair is not an identity mapping returning the input, but instead plays a significant role in the forecast construction. Third, by examining increments of individual processor blocks across model depth, we show that all three models progressively refine the forecast from coarse to finer spatial scales. Finally, we assess the physical consistency of the intermediate decoding forecasts and find that large scales remain physically balanced throughout processing, while small scales become more balanced with each additional processor block.

title: Do LMs Know What Variables Do? Interpreting Code Representations via Variable Roles
comments: 46 pages, 25 figures
abstract: Variable roles describe recurring behaviors such as accumulation, traversal, and retaining the best candidate encountered. We use Sajaniemi's independently defined taxonomy to study which role distinctions can be recovered from large language models, how sparse autoencoders (SAEs) retain those distinctions, and whether associated directions support control of generation. We introduce static annotation rules for all eleven roles and a corpus of 126,926 natural-code files across five languages. Across five model-SAE systems, residual probes outperform individual SAE features and tested lexical baselines, with modest losses after neutral target renaming. Combining SAE features closes much of the single-feature gap, but probes on SAE reconstructions are less sensitive to role-changing edits reviewed by LLMs. High paired ranking accuracy coexists with frequent false positives at fixed thresholds. During generation, interventions often change role annotations at the cost of correctness; changes accompanied by passing tests show no clear aggregate advantage over random controls. The benchmark separates role-related recoverability, SAE fidelity, and correctness-preserving control through matched prediction, source edits, and generation interventions.

title: Recording-Aware Evaluation of Multimodal OT Intrusion Detection
comments: 12 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for presentation at the Industrial Control System Security Workshop (ICSS 2026), held in conjunction with the IEEE Annual Computer Security Applications Conference (ACSAC 2026), Los Angeles, CA, USA, December 2026. Code and results are available at: this https URL
abstract: Machine-learning-based intrusion detection systems (IDSs) for operational technology (OT) are commonly evaluated on benchmark datasets in which normal and attack data are collected in separate recordings. In such settings, high performance may reflect recording-associated differences as well as attack behavior. We introduce a recording-aware evaluation procedure that compares attack windows with background from the same recording, uses prior data for model fitting and calibration, tests temporal alignment against randomized event schedules, and reports event coverage together with alarm burden. On the ProvICS multimodal dataset, cyber modalities strongly distinguish the benign and attack recordings before the first labeled attack. Same-recording evaluation reverses the apparent modality ranking across all studied window sizes: the physical view becomes the strongest individual modality, while cyber-only fusion shows the largest difference between cross-recording and same-recording AUC, reaching 0.54. Operational analysis further shows that permissive event-overlap metrics can overstate detection when a small number of long alarm episodes cover multiple actions. An external analysis on HAI shows smaller and reference-dependent recording sensitivity. These findings show that cross-recording benchmark performance should be interpreted alongside same-recording, forward, temporal, and operational evaluations.

title: Reducing double-dipping in single-cell topic models with three-way count splitting
comments: 16 pages, 4 figures. Code: this https URL
abstract: Topic models learn gene programs from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data, and the same counts are then used to test which genes and donors are associated with those programs. Count splitting is the standard remedy for this reuse, but it has not been tested when an encoder reads each cell's counts. On a 104,400-cell lupus cohort with 300 permuted null genes per run, naive tests rejected 36% of null gene-topic pairs at a nominal 5% level, and the usual two-way split rejected 38%, because the encoder sees the tested gene's own held-out count. Encoding topic usage on a separate third of the counts, with beta-binomial thinning, lowered this to 7.7% (6.7% for genes outside the model); for two other models, LDVAE and scETM, the rate was 7.0-7.3% (naive 51-59%). A label-free interferon program shifts in held-out counts in the lupus cohort and in a pre-specified COVID-19 cohort, and donor-level topic usage predicts disease (AUROC 0.96) beyond cell-type proportions (0.86 and 0.58 in the two cohorts). Calibration and prediction did not depend on the model. We do not claim better clustering, prediction or topic stability. Code, figures and result tables are public (MIT license; DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23307193).

title: Sequence-to-Sequence Neural Surrogate Modeling of Transient Responses in High-Speed Links with Variable Design Parameters
comments: 12 pages, 13 figures, 5 tables. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
subjects: Signal Processing (eess.SP); Computational Engineering, Finance, and Science (cs.CE); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: This paper presents sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) neural surrogates for high-speed transient response modeling and signal integrity analysis in fixed and variable design parameter spaces. To identify the structural requirements for prediction accuracy, multiple neural architectures were evaluated with respect to different training strategies such as sample-based and unit interval-based, as well as input configurations such as TX-only and TX+RX. For fixed design parameters, feedforward neural networks achieve accuracy comparable to recurrent models while requiring lower computational cost, as the static mapping can be approximated by fully connected and non-sequential representations. Variable design parameters alter the electromagnetic characteristics of the interconnect, which creates parameter-dependent temporal dynamics that require sequence-aware architectures to resolve the evolving interactions within the transient response. The results based on a 14-dimensional variable design parameter scenario show that while autoregressive TX+RX feedback suffers from severe phase drift and error propagation under variable conditions, non-autoregressive TX-only inference leads to stability. To overcome the structural limitations of standard decoders, a recurrent Early Fusion LSTM is proposed, which injects design parameters at the initial encoding stage. This approach achieves superior prediction accuracy, with an RMSE of 31.0 mV and an R2 of 99.51% for transient waveform prediction, an RMSE of 30.7 mV and an R2 of 99.57% for eye-height prediction, and an RMSE of 19.5 ps and an R2 of 99.94% for eye-width prediction. These results demonstrate that neural seq2seq surrogates are accurate for transient response modeling and signal integrity analysis in complex variable design parameter spaces.

title: Candidate-dependent residual routing trades top-of-list accuracy for recall in sequential recommendation
comments: 33 pages, 3 figures. Includes 18 pages of Supplemental Information with 18 supplementary tables
abstract: Candidate-dependent routing lets a sequential recommender weight a user's past behaviors differently for each item it scores. We test whether this flexibility helps by adding a small residual routing module to a self-attentive baseline, in two versions that differ only in what sets the routing weights: the user's history representation or the candidate item's embedding. Across five paired seeds on the REES46 cosmetics-shop dataset, with matched training for all three models, candidate-dependent routing leaves the primary metric, normalized discounted cumulative gain at cutoff ten (NDCG@10), essentially unchanged (mean relative change +0.003%). Secondary and exploratory analyses show that this flat average hides two effects that cancel. The candidate-dependent model places more relevant items in its top ten (recall +1.81%) but ranks the first one lower (mean reciprocal rank -1.09%), and most of its new hits land at positions six to ten. Its gains come from queries with at least one target among the user's last 50 events, while queries whose targets all lie outside that window get worse. In this form, candidate-dependent routing trades accuracy at the top of the list for recall further down.

title: Certified neural approximations for parabolic obstacle problems
subjects: Numerical Analysis (math.NA); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Functional Analysis (math.FA)
abstract: Residual-trained neural surrogates carry no error guarantee, a limitation for free-boundary problems such as phase change and contact. We derive guaranteed error bounds for neural approximations of parabolic obstacle problems in first-order state--flux--multiplier form. The main result bounds the flux error of the network and the energy error of its feasible projection $\max\{v,g\}$ by the constitutive residual, the initial mismatch, the complementarity defect, and the PDE residual weighted by $c_F^2/\alpha$, without the coercivity and norm-equivalence constants of the first-order formulation. It extends the Apushkinskaya--Repin majorant for the heat operator to general coefficients, free multipliers and a flux bound. A penetration-consistency result shows that neural triples with arbitrarily small bound exist. Outward-rounded cellwise Taylor-model enclosures turn the bound into a finite computation valid on any adaptive partition. The flux and gradient errors of the projected output are certified below $0.27$ and $0.33$ of the solution scale for a one-dimensional Stefan problem and, after adaptive refinement, below one half for all three trained networks on a two-dimensional expanding disk. On an expanding ellipse the gradient bound stays above one half; substitution diagnostics trace the floor of the trained networks to the projected state near the free boundary, and the remaining gap to enclosure overhead. Without a closed-form solution, a validated lower bound replaces the solution norm; there the enclosure is nearly exact, but the trained networks have errors above the solution scale and no useful accuracy is certified. The bounds control a state--flux norm, not the multiplier or the free-boundary location.

title: Censored Flow Matching for Synthetic Time-to-Event Generation
subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computation (stat.CO); Methodology (stat.ME)
abstract: Generating time-to-event data is increasingly important in survival analysis, but it remains statistically challenging because event times are often censored and thus prevent flexible generative modeling. To fill this gap, we propose a novel method called censored flow matching (CFM), aiming at providing a flexible flow-based generative mechanism for synthesizing time-to-event data as well as learning their corresponding probabilistic densities. Unlike existing methods, CFM does not rely on survival likelihoods to handle censoring, but instead exploits the monotonicity property of differential flows to address censoring via pullback sampling. Under this framework, we implement an alternating procedure between pullback sampling and CFM steps, leading to a flow-based expectation--maximization (EM) algorithm tailored for time-to-event inference. Under mild distributional conditions, we establish the convergence of CFM to the true event-time distribution as the EM iterations proceed. We then apply CFM to generate time-to-event data and estimate their probabilistic densities, where the observed censoring time can be incorporated to provide truncated sampling or truncated density estimation for survival inference. Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate the benefits of CFM for complex and large-scale data generation. Finally, we apply CFM to analyze data from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) and the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV), showcasing its benefits for synthetic and predictive survival analyses in terms of data fidelity, predictive performance, and empirical privacy characteristics.

title: Preserving Reasoning Diversity in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards via Adaptive Replay
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but often reduces the diversity of their reasoning behaviors. We study this phenomenon from the perspective of finite-sample learning dynamics and show that limited on-policy rollouts can progressively suppress semantically distinct but equally rewarded reasoning modes. Once a mode becomes sufficiently under-sampled, standard on-policy RLVR rarely recovers it. Motivated by this observation, we propose TAR, a Targeted Adaptive Replay framework that preserves diverse correct reasoning behaviors already present in the base policy. TAR constructs a compact memory bank of diverse base-model solutions and selectively replays them through an adaptive mechanism that activates only when stored behaviors are being suppressed during RLVR. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two Qwen2.5 model scales, TAR consistently achieves a better balance between reasoning performance and diversity preservation than existing diversity-preserving post-training methods, while substantially reducing the forgetting of correct base-model solutions. Code is available at this https URL.

title: Extending Myerson's Optimal Auctions to Correlated Bidders via Neural Network Interpolation
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
subjects: Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Theoretical Economics (econ.TH)
abstract: We aim to design revenue-maximizing single-item auctions that are deterministic, strategy-proof, and ex post individually rational --- the quintessential fundamental model for optimal mechanism design. While Myerson's seminal work solved this model for independent bidders, straightforward extensions to correlated settings often result in non-monotonic, and therefore non-strategy-proof allocations. Critically, optimal allocation design for correlated bidders is NP-hard to approximate, rendering theoretical optimality guarantees in this domain computationally intractable. We establish a new standard of empirical rigor for this theoretically hard model by proposing an empirical pipeline. We synthesize neural interpolation of Myerson's greedy allocation based on marginal profits (the correlated variant of virtual valuation), formal neural verification to enforce exact strategy-proofness, and a constructive repair procedure. Empirically, our method is highly effective, consistently achieves near-optimal revenue across a wide range of distributions, including synthetic, adversarial, and real-world (consumer, financial, and industrial) datasets. Compared to existing manual and neural baselines, our approach shows substantial improvement, often reducing the revenue gap by an order of magnitude. Our study is also the first to introduce (unattainable) greedy revenue as a rigorous upper bound for empirical benchmarking, providing a definitive quantitative performance measure where true optima remain theoretically elusive. We demonstrate the generality of our approach by extending it to multi-unit auctions with unit demand and integrating our verification techniques into RegretNet to achieve exact strategy-proofness.

title: CoCoNet: Convex Conformal Network for Multi-Dimensional Uncertainty Regions
abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free coverage guarantees under exchangeability, but the efficiency of its prediction regions depends critically on the choice of the conformity score. This is particularly important in multivariate regression, where dependencies across output dimensions induce complex joint uncertainty structures. This paper introduces CoCoNet (Convex Conformal Network) for learning convex conformity scores that induce flexible, data-adaptive prediction regions. CoCoNet learns the score from held-out data by optimizing prediction-region efficiency while enforcing convexity with respect to the residual. CoCoNet then applies split-conformal calibration to retain finite-sample coverage guarantees. The paper presents two variants of the method: CoCoNet$_{\mathrm{Spline}}$, based on piecewise-linear scores, and CoCoNet$_{\mathrm{ICNN}}$, based on Input Convex Neural Networks. Experiments compare CoCoNet with other CP baselines over synthetic and real-world datasets with output dimensions ranging from 2 to 16. The results demonstrate the flexibility of CoCoNet in learning different response types. Across 8 models and 30 multi-dimensional regression tasks, CoCoNet$_\text{ICNN}$ and CoCoNet$_{\mathrm{Spline}\text{-}\ell_1}$ achieve the best efficiencies with average ranks of 1.45 and 2.75, respectively. In particular, CoCoNet$_\text{ICNN}$ ranks first on 22 tasks out of 30 in terms of efficiency.

title: Can This LLM Annotate My Data? Estimating Zero-Shot LLM Performance
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in annotation tasks with varying success. While several studies have demonstrated the opportunities and shortcomings of LLMs for annotation, a critical question remains unanswered: is it possible to predict how well they will perform on a new dataset? To answer this and related questions, we construct two task families which induce 461 text classification datasets. We find that it is possible to predict LLM performance - to a certain degree - and that contrary to other work which highlights the usefulness of LLM verbalizations of self-confidence, internal log-probabilities are the most predictive signal.

title: BanglaShield: A Script-Robust Safety Classifier and Benchmark for Bangla Native, Romanized, and Code-Mixed Prompts
comments: 17 pages. Code and data: this https URL ; dataset: this https URL
abstract: Safety classifiers for large language models (LLMs) are typically built and evaluated on standard-script text, yet Bangla, like many lower-resource languages, is routinely written in native script, in Latin-script romanization, and code-mixed with English, Hindi, or Urdu. We introduce BanglaShield, a resource and model for graded prompt-safety classification across these written forms. We consolidate 10,245 Bangla prompts from six sources under a four-level taxonomy (Safe, Offensive, Harmful, Severe) and render each prompt in three aligned forms that share labels and a group-aware split, enabling strictly paired comparisons. Benchmarking six contemporary LLMs, including a Bangla-specialized one, on 36,882 classification queries and 24,318 judged responses, we find that LLM classifiers label 47.0% of unsafe native-script prompts as Safe, rising to 63.4% under romanization, while response-level safety accuracy drops by 10.3 points. Three multilingual guard models also pass 30.3-57.3% of unsafe native-script prompts. Using a model's own classification as an input filter reduces harmful compliance by only about five points. In contrast, BanglaShield, a compact fine-tuned encoder, reaches 87.8 macro-F1 on native-script and 84.4 on romanized prompts, outperforming the best LLM on each form by 42.8-46.1 points with ~130x fewer parameters than Gemma 4 31B. We release the corpus, splits, judgments, and model.

title: What Matters for NVFP4 Training? A Comparative Study of Low-Precision Pretraining Recipes
comments: 10 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Resource-Adaptive Foundation Model Inference (AdaptFM), Seoul, South Korea
subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Training large language models directly in 4-bit floating-point (FP) formats promises substantial improvements in throughput and energy efficiency. While some recipe design choices have been validated at scale, many promising approaches remain untested beyond small models and short token horizons, leaving open the question of which trends will hold. We present a systematic comparison of recent NVFP4 recipes at medium model scale, evaluating dense 8B and 30B-A3B MoE models trained for up to 1T tokens, with a focus on which ingredients are necessary for accuracy recovery. We propose a final recipe grounded in the principles behind established stable NVFP4 training at scale, incorporating state-of-the-art techniques such as unbiased gradient estimation with lower quantization error than stochastic rounding. To the best of our knowledge, this is the strongest FP4 training result demonstrated at this scale to date in loss gap to BF16. Through ablation studies, we find that: (i) each technique in the optimized recipe measurably improves loss trajectory, (ii) selective high-precision layers are necessary for recovering accuracy at scale, (iii) not all tensors in the backward pass benefit equally from de-biasing, leaving room to apply complementary error-reduction techniques to the remaining tensors.

title: Blackbox Performance Analysis of LLM-based Network Control
subjects: Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: LLMs are becoming an indispensable part of network control systems due to their impressive reasoning. Before such LLM-enabled systems can be deployed, it is imperative to develop tools that can audit their performance on previously unseen inputs. However, auditing these systems is challenging due to the inherent opacity of LLMs. LENS is the first step towards black-box performance analysis of LLM-enabled network control systems. It uses novel methods to extend deep reinforcement learning to guide the search for performance gaps and inputs that make LLMs struggle. LENS finds large gaps for LLM-based traffic engineering and GPU allocation systems, and even matches existing white-box analyzers designed for hand-crafted TE heuristics.

title: Can Agents Keep Secrets They Were Never Told? Benchmarking Latent Privacy Risks Across Sessions with MemJoin
abstract: To support sustained interactions and personalized assistance, agents use long-term memory to retain and combine user information across sessions. Reusing such memories can lead an agent to state a sensitive relation while completing an ordinary task that does not require it. The relation to protect and the combination of clues that reveal it may remain hidden at memory write time, when later records and tasks are still unknown. In this paper, we introduce MemJoin, a privacy benchmark of 288 synthetic analysis cases in which the complete history entails a sensitive relation, but every individual session is insufficient. We evaluate six memory systems with the same answer-generating model, alongside full-history and no-history controls. Each system writes and updates memories in session order and later retrieves context for an ordinary task, while target annotations remain with the evaluator. We separately check which target attribute values appear in stored records and retrieved context, and whether the final answer states the complete, person-linked relation. In a separate paired test on a prespecified subset, removing shared identifiers and other connecting clues can change complete-relation output while all checked target attribute values remain visible. These findings show why checking attribute visibility alone is insufficient to evaluate what records from different sessions reveal together.

title: A decomposition-integration framework coupling singular spectrum analysis with a volatility-adaptive LSTM for stock price forecasting
subjects: Computational Engineering, Finance, and Science (cs.CE); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Financial time series exhibit multi-scale, high-noise, and non-stationary volatility dynamics. Decomposition--integration frameworks built on complete ensemble empirical mode decomposition with adaptive noise (CEEMDAN) have advanced this field, yet existing CEEMDAN hybrids remain unstable: high-frequency mode mixing contaminates downstream predictors, and the heterogeneous volatility of decomposed components is not matched by any volatility-adaptive mechanism. To address these gaps, this paper proposes CEEMDAN-SE-SSA-VMGL. CEEMDAN adaptively decomposes the original series, and sample-entropy-driven K-means clustering groups the intrinsic mode functions into high-, mid-, and low-frequency and residual components. Singular spectrum analysis (SSA) is then applied to the high-frequency group, whose singular-value decomposition of the trajectory matrix and principal-component reconstruction decouple intertwined pseudo-oscillatory modes and alleviate mode mixing. We further design a plug-and-play robust LSTM variant, the volatility-modulated GARCH-LSTM (VMGL), which embeds a differentiable GARCH(1,1) layer inside the LSTM cell as a risk gate; the estimated conditional volatility multiplicatively scales the forget-gate activation, letting memory decay adapt to the instantaneous volatility while remaining fully end-to-end trainable. Component predictions are linearly combined. On five US and Chinese financial series (CSI 300, CSI 500, AAPL, GOOGL, S&P 500), the proposed model is compared with eleven benchmark architectures, lowering the forecasting error by 9% to 24% relative to the best benchmark and by 60% to 70% relative to a standard LSTM. Diebold--Mariano and model-confidence-set (MCS) tests confirm the statistical significance and stability of the gains, spectral analyses verify the SSA denoising efficacy, and backtesting demonstrates the framework's economic utility.

title: Learning volatility-adaptive forgetting via GARCH-modulated LSTM for stock price forecasting
subjects: Computational Engineering, Finance, and Science (cs.CE); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Stock price forecasting is hindered by the heteroscedastic nature of financial time series, in which turbulent and tranquil regimes alternate. Although the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network is widely used for this task, its gates are oblivious to such volatility variation, so memory retention remains fixed regardless of market conditions. A common remedy is to supply volatility estimates as an additional input feature, yet this leaves the internal memory dynamics untouched. Instead, volatility can serve as a direct regulatory signal over the gate activation itself. This paper presents the Gsigmoid-LSTM model, which embeds Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity (GARCH(1,1))-derived volatility estimates into the LSTM forgetting gate through the Gsigmoid activation function, a volatility-adaptive variant of the sigmoid that combines a volatility adjustment factor with slope regulation via a learnable parameter. The model thereby automatically prioritizes recent information during turbulent periods while preserving long-term dependencies in stable markets. In the engineering application of daily stock price forecasting, extensive experiments, including activation function comparisons, baseline evaluations, and ablation studies, demonstrate that this structural gating modification effectively improves forecasting accuracy and robustness. The proposed model significantly outperforms a feature-level fusion baseline carrying the same volatility signal on all five datasets, as confirmed by Diebold-Mariano tests with all p<0.01, attains the best average rank of 1.00 in the Friedman test across nine models, and achieves the lowest MSE and MAE on all five datasets.

title: Prototype-Guided Optimization of Quantum Data Embeddings with Linear Cost
comments: 26 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables
abstract: In supervised quantum machine learning with classical data, classification performance critically depends on the geometry induced by quantum data embedding. Existing data-adaptive approaches rely on pairwise fidelity evaluations between samples, which scale as $O(B^2)$ for $B$ samples and create a computational bottleneck in iterative embedding optimization. To address this issue, we propose a prototype-guided framework for efficient data-adaptive quantum embedding. Using class-prototype separation and sample-to-prototype compactness, we derive a measurable lower certificate for class-ensemble distinguishability and construct a prototype-based objective requiring only $O(B)$ fidelity evaluations. We integrate this objective into an end-to-end pipeline that combines task-specific quantum circuit architecture optimization with continuous refinement of the data-embedding parameters. Across five benchmark datasets with up to 20 qubits, our method retains competitive quantum kernel support vector machine (SVM) performance while reducing fidelity-evaluation cost, with particularly strong gains over budget-matched pairwise optimization on T-MNIST. Geometric analyses examine how the learned embeddings relate to kernel alignment and classification margins, revealing dataset-dependent benefits and limitations. We further derive a prototype-based classifier in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space that provides an explicit witness for the SVM objective and a low-cost proxy for model selection, and extend the framework to multiple prototypes for multimodal class structures.

title: Margin-Based Generalization for Quantum Machine Learning with Classical Data Encoding
comments: 22 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables
abstract: Understanding generalization is essential for assessing the practical viability of quantum machine learning. In many applications, quantum models operate on classical data that must first be encoded into quantum states, making the encoding part of the effective hypothesis class. We develop a margin-based generalization framework for this setting, covering both fixed and trainable quantum data encodings. For fixed encodings, the existing margin bound transfers unchanged. For trainable encodings, we derive a bound using a two-scale covering argument that combines the original margin-dependent term with an additive encoding-capacity term of order $\tilde O(\sqrt{L/m})$, where $L$ is the number of trainable encoding parameters and $m$ is the training-sample size. Across 19,440 simulated training runs spanning various image datasets, circuit architectures, and optimization settings, the inverse margin performs best among five baseline and two bound-derived complexity measures under conditional-independence and 90th-percentile sign-error criteria, within bootstrap uncertainty. These results provide a unified margin-based view of generalization in quantum machine learning with classical data.

title: Private Evaluation of High-Dimensional Functions
subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Information Theory (cs.IT); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: We study differentially private black-box evaluation of arbitrary high-dimensional functions. Given a dataset $S$ and query access to a function $f$---whose sensitivity may be unknown or unbounded---the goal is to privately output an approximation to $f(S)$. The black-box evaluator can only query the value of $f$ over a down neighborhood of $S$ (i.e., those subsets of $S$ that are obtained by removing a bounded number of elements from $S$). We design generic black-box evaluators for both pure and approximate differential privacy through a reduction to high-dimensional private quasi-concave optimization (QCO). Our black-box evaluator enjoys a geometric notion of utility. Consider the vectors obtained by applying $f$ on sets in a down neighborhood of $S$. With high probability, the evaluator's output is guaranteed to be in the convex hull of these vectors. Our work generalizes the result of Linder et al. [LRSS25] for real-valued function evaluation to high dimensions. It also recovers the private center-point guarantees of Beimel et al. [BMNS19], with an explicit additive approximation to maximum Tukey depth. We also apply our evaluators to user-level quasi-concave and convex optimization, showing how they can improve upon the sample-and-aggregate baseline of Nissim et al. [NRS07] by replacing the multiplicative data overhead with an additive overhead. Finally, we show that our formulation of high dimensional black-box evaluation and high dimensional private QCO are equivalent up to a factor of the dimension: the hardest private evaluation instances already arise from the cases that $f$ is a (non-private) quasi-concave optimizer.

title: Denoising Implicit Variational Inference
comments: Neurips 2026 camera ready
abstract: Semi-implicit variational inference (SIVI) expands the representational capacity of variational families, but optimizing the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) remains challenging because the marginal score of the semi-implicit distribution is generally intractable. Unbiased Implicit Variational Inference (UIVI) and related methods address this difficulty through reparameterized ELBO gradients, but existing approaches estimate the required score indirectly through reverse-conditional sampling or approximation, which can be computationally costly and unstable. We propose Denoising Implicit Variational Inference (DIVI), which learns the marginal score directly via denoising score matching. The learned score is used as a plug-in estimator in the pathwise ELBO gradient, replacing inner reverse-conditional sampling with a score-network evaluation. We analyze DIVI as inexact stochastic gradient ascent and show, under stated assumptions, that the averaged stationarity measure is controlled by the usual optimization term and the average score-matching error. Empirically, we evaluate DIVI on both synthetic distributions and a variety of real-data Bayesian inference tasks. The results show that DIVI improves over the current UIVI baselines while reducing the cost of ELBO-gradient estimation.

title: Reconstruction of Unobserved Core Electron Density in Tokamak Plasmas with a Neural Operator Transport Surrogate and Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Real-time control of tokamak plasmas requires the electron density profile. However, in a reactor-relevant device, diagnostic port access is limited and the profile can be observed only partially. In the present work we reconstruct the density profile by inferring the coefficients of a physics-based one-dimensional particle transport equation, using a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) surrogate of the transport solver as a fast differentiable forward model. The surrogate enables realtime-compatible gradient-based reconstruction and uncertainty quantification from the reflectometry and interferometry measurements. We compare four uncertainty quantification methods - multi-seed ensembles, the Laplace approximation, Metropolis-Hastings, and a Gaussian method independent of the reconstruction fit. The resulting uncertainty is scored with CRPS and coverage calibration, separately on the observed and unobserved regions. We further demonstrate advantage of our approach over standard analytical function fit on synthetic and experimental DIII-D discharges.

title: Contrastive Hypergraph Source-free Domain Adaptive Object Detection in Adverse Weather Conditions--Extended Version
comments: 20 pages. An extended version of "Contrastive Hypergraph Source-free Domain Adaptive Object Detection in Adverse Weather Conditions" accepted at NeurIPS 2026
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Adverse weather conditions such as fog, rain, snow, and low illumination introduce structured visibility degradations that severely impair object detectors trained on clear-weather data. When source data are inaccessible due to privacy or trans- mission constraints, source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) becomes necessary. However, existing SFDA methods based on pairwise contrastive learning struggle to capture high-order semantics and often suffer from agreement collapse under severe corruption. We propose REUNION, a hypergraph-guided SFDA framework for object detection in adverse weather conditions. REUNION constructs a contrastive hypergraph over target-domain object proposals, encoding high-order relations through intra-image context, weather-aware grouping, prototype-based semantic anchors, and uncertainty-aware connections between reliable and low-confidence instances. To effectively exploit these structured relations, we introduce a group-wise Hyper-InfoNCE objective that optimizes representations at the hyperedge level, enabling semantic information to propagate from confident proposals to corrupted or low-contrast instances. Experiments with diverse benchmarks demonstrate that REUNION effectively mitigates domain shifts and achieves state-of-the-art performance in SFDA settings.

title: Accelerating Finite-Sum Bilevel Optimization with Fully First-Order Oracles
comments: 23 pages, 2 figures, 1 table
subjects: Optimization and Control (math.OC); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Machine Learning (stat.ML)
abstract: We study nonconvex--strongly-convex bilevel optimization with finite-sum objectives and fully first-order oracles. We propose Sampled Implicit Corrections for Bilevel Optimization (SICBO), which combines a penalty approximation with variance-reduced corrections for the lower-level variables. Under componentwise lower strong convexity, SICBO finds a point $x$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi(x)\|^2\le\varepsilon^2$ within $\tilde{O}(N+\sqrt{N}\kappa^{7/2}\varepsilon^{-2})$ component-gradient calls, where $N$ is the total number of components and $\kappa$ is the normalized lower-level condition number. The bound achieves square-root finite-sum dependence using only gradients and preserves the best known deterministic fully first-order condition-number exponent for smooth problems. Our improvement follows from a curvature-dependent bound for nonlinear correction errors, which permits epochs of length $\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N/\kappa})$ with batches of size $\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N\kappa})$. A single-level reduction shows that the dependence on $N$ and $\varepsilon$ is optimal up to logarithmic factors for fixed $\kappa$.

title: ASR Personalization in Pathological Voice: Accuracy, Efficiency, and Duration Effects
comments: Presented at SPECOM 2026
subjects: Sound (cs.SD); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Audio and Speech Processing (eess.AS)
abstract: Automatic Speech recognition (ASR) struggles with Pathological speech due to persistent speaker-specific mismatch. In clinical and accessibility scenarios, only limited target-speaker data is typically available, making full model retraining impractical. We present a component-level analysis of LoRA adaptation in Whisper, investigating how adapter placement interacts with the model size, training efficiency and utterance-duration in single-speaker settings. Our experimental comparative study shows that while scaling reduces errors, it does not eliminate mismatch. Furthermore, the full attention LoRa provides the most reliable accuracy, and the best time--accuracy trade-off. Improvements vary across utterance length, with medium-length recordings benefiting the most, while short and long utterances remain challenging. These findings highlight the importance of adaptation placement and duration-dependent evaluation, under challenging, data-scarce personalization scenarios.

title: Conditional Weight of Evidence for Gradient-Boosted Credit Models: Estimation, Additivity and Its Relation to Adverse Action Reasons
comments: 41 pages, 3 figures, 12 tables. Code: this https URL
subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Risk Management (q-fin.RM); Methodology (stat.ME)
abstract: Traditional weight of evidence assigns a credit characteristic a value based on its association with default across a population. Credit analysis also requires an assessment of that characteristic in the context of an individual applicant's record. We study conditional weight of evidence for this purpose. It measures the change in default log odds from observing a characteristic after the remaining credit information is known. Its sign identifies whether the characteristic adds adverse or favorable information for that applicant, and its magnitude measures the strength of that information. The same characteristic value can therefore receive different assessments for applicants with different payment histories or other credit attributes. We develop estimators using gradient-boosted trees and evaluate their accuracy in a bureau-style simulation. Regressions of the full model's predicted probabilities recover conditional evidence more accurately than separate models fitted to default outcomes, provided the full model is accurate. They also recover a deliberately constructed file-age effect whose direction varies with utilization and is often missed by marginal weight of evidence. Local class-frequency estimates improve on marginal weight of evidence but remain inaccurate for some weak effects. An application to FICO HELOC data illustrates estimation when the population evidence is unknown. Conditional weight of evidence provides an applicant-specific interpretation of the information in a credit characteristic; its population summary, a conditional information value, splits the joint information in the record across blocks when averaged over orderings. Neither is an adverse action reason, which explains the fitted score difference between the applicant and chosen passing records.

title: Training with Ciphers to Enhance In-Context Terminology Learning For Translation from Rare Languages
abstract: Fine-tuning LLMs with in-context examples (IC-Train) lets translation models adapt to new parallel data at deployment, but it is unclear whether they actually learn the translations of rare terms from those examples. We formalize this capability as in-context term learning (ICTL). We show that standard IC-Train develops this capability only weakly, and propose RareCipherFT, which strengthens it without any lexical resources. RareCipherFT pairs each training target with in-context examples that share a rare term with it. It then replaces that term with a character-shuffled cipher in both the context and the reference, so the term can only be recovered by copying from context. The ciphered fraction of training data is annealed to preserve translation quality. Across seven translation directions between English and Tamil, Assamese, Mizo, Nepali and Hausa, and four models from 1B to 7B parameters, RareCipherFT raises term recall over standard IC-Train by 5-15 absolute points without lowering COMET. Probes using synonyms, nonce words and controls for shared surface context show that these gains come from linking source terms to their in-context translations rather than from shortcuts.

title: Modeling Uncertainty Propagation in 3D Morphable Models
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: We study the problem of mapping parameter-space variance of a 3D Morphable Model (3DMM) to per-vertex variance. Traditionally, per-vertex variance has been used to visually interpret the learnt parameter uncertainty. However, mapping parameter-space variance to per-vertex using sampling or error propagation is computationally expensive. We address this limitation with Closed-form Local Uncertainty Estimation (CLUE), which transforms the parameter-space distribution of 3DMMs to per-vertex through a closed-form approximation. CLUE emerges from applying the law of total variance to the 3DMM formulation and is modular, computationally inexpensive, and accurate. Subsequently, we study integrating CLUE for in-the-wild human mesh recovery training and inference. We note that CLUE uses the geometry of the mesh as an inductive bias when predicting the variance, leading to improved accuracy. Through extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments, we show that when used in training, CLUE (1) outpeforms probabilistic and deterministic baselines on metrics evaluating joints, mesh and uncertainty, and (2) has the highest uncertainty-to-error spearman correlation, with applications including data mining and interpretable uncertainty. Finally, we share SAM 3D Body (CLUE) which augments the regressor with high resolution uncertainty maps. We make our code available at this https URL

title: Lightweight Machine Learning for Classifying Disaster-Related Social Media Posts
subjects: Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Classifying disaster-related social-media posts into humanitarian information labels is challenging because individual messages are typically short and context-limited, humanitarian categories can overlap semantically, and the CrisisBench label distribution is strongly imbalanced. This study investigates whether lightweight lexical machine-learning methods can provide effective and computationally efficient classification under these conditions. Using the CrisisBench v1.0 English humanitarian task, comprising 87,455 records across predefined Train, Development and Test splits, we conduct a controlled comparison of TF-IDF representations and lightweight classifiers, with Macro-F1 as the primary model-selection metric. Beyond aggregate predictive performance, the study jointly examines per-label behaviour, directional error patterns, relative decision margins, computational requirements, and the effect of domain-specific training through a tropical-cyclone specialist model. The selected balanced LinearSVC with unigram-bigram TF-IDF and C=0.5 achieved an Accuracy of 0.8282, a Macro-F1 of 0.6578 and a Weighted-F1 of 0.8315 on the held-out Test split. Lower decision margins were substantially associated with prediction errors, while the tropical-cyclone specialist achieved modestly higher in-domain aggregate performance with substantially lower feature and fitting requirements. The study contributes a controlled, label-sensitive and resource-aware evaluation of lightweight humanitarian text classification that characterises not only aggregate performance, but also where these models fail and how their behaviour changes under domain-specific training.

title: What RL Brings to Reasoning: A Few Decisions the Base Model Would Not Make
comments: 26 Pages, 8 figures Code: this https URL
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) substantially improves mathematical reasoning, but what it adds to the base model remains unclear. We investigate this through a sequence of generation-time interventions on Qwen3-4B-Base, measuring how much of its RL-trained counterpart's gain each intervention recovers on 120 AIME problems. Power sampling with the same 8,192-token output limit brings no gain beyond greedy decoding. Yet borrowing the RL model's token only where the two models' greedy choices differ, roughly 4% of generated positions, recovers 90.5% of the pass@1 gain, with similar recovery across three model pairs on MATH-500. We find that even a single opening token has a substantial effect: forcing the base model to begin with "Alright" recovers 35% of the RL gain. The opening alone is insufficient, however. Later replacements after the same opening add another 5.2 percentage points to pass@1, and the fixed rules we test for inserting reflective words such as "Wait" do not reproduce this benefit. Sparse replacement also retains much of the base model's diversity while staying close to the RL model at pass@1. At k=256, it solves 67.5% of the problems, significantly more than the RL model (61.4%) and a mixture of whole responses matched in pass@1 (61.45%). The comparison is at equal attempt counts rather than equal compute, since rl-replace consults both models at every decoding step. These results show that the opening can recover a meaningful part of the RL gain, but a larger contribution comes from later choices, which can be borrowed while retaining much of the base model's diversity. Code is available at this https URL.

title: MM-LeJEPA: Correlated Gaussian Regularization for Multimodal Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures
abstract: LeJEPA derives an isotropic Gaussian embedding target by minimizing, under its task assumptions, a Fisher information criterion that controls the task-averaged squared prediction bias. This enables unimodal self-supervised learning without reconstruction decoders, exponential-moving-average teachers, or contrastive negatives. However, its isotropic task prior does not account for the cross-modal structure of multimodal tasks that read shared content. We introduce MM-LeJEPA by extending LeJEPA's task assumptions to multimodal learning. Specifically, we model multimodal tasks as strength-weighted combinations of components that read independent information from the two modalities and components that read the same content from both. Under explicit gradient-moment, correspondence, and symmetry assumptions, we derive a correlated Gaussian target that minimizes a weighted Fisher information functional under a fixed total variance constraint. An analytic transform adapts Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg) to this target, yielding a two-term objective that combines distributional regularization with local-to-global prediction. The extension adds a single scalar hyperparameter, the target cross-modal correlation, and retains the simplicity of LeJEPA. On public audio-visual classification benchmarks, our results are competitive with representative open-source methods. Code will be released.

title: Spherical Physics-informed Neural Operator with Multi-scale Coupling for Meteorological Downscaling
comments: Published in IJCAI 2026 (AI4Tech: AI Enabling Technologies). 9 pages, 4 figures
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Atmospheric and Oceanic Physics (physics.ao-ph)
abstract: Meteorological downscaling is crucial for high-resolution regional climate forecasting and disaster early warning. While neural operators have emerged as a promising paradigm for modeling complex spatiotemporal mappings, existing frameworks often struggle with spherical manifold geometric distortions, inherent atmospheric multi-scale coupling mismatches, and lack of explicit atmospheric laws. We propose the Spherical Physics-informed Neural Operator, which utilizes a Spherical Laplacian Decomposition to partition atmospheric fields into hierarchical frequency components, maintaining exact point-wise correspondence across scales. To evaluate these representations at arbitrary locations, we introduce a localized spherical integral operator that approximates continuous kernel transforms via geometry-aware attention. Dynamical consistency is further enforced by embedding differentiable constraints into the learning process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework attains superior accuracy and zero-shot generalization across various meteorological variables and unseen queries, representing a robust and interpretable solution for global-to-regional meteorological downscaling.

title: When Do Repetition Loops Lock? Truncation Sampling, Bounded Penalties, and a Blind Spot in DRY
comments: 17 pages, 5 figures
abstract: Language models sometimes repeat verbatim until the generation limit. We study the exit rather than the entrance: given that a span has already been repeated $n$ times, when is escape still possible? Along the loop the context is deterministic, so loop survival under any sampler can be computed exactly from one forward pass. Pure sampling leaves a positive escape probability at every step; top-$p$ with threshold $\pi>1/2$ locks a position exactly when the continuation probability reaches $\pi$. A bounded penalty can leave a position locked; a penalty that outgrows the model's preference for the loop over unseen tokens guarantees escape under top-$p$. The same analysis predicts a blind spot in the widely deployed DRY sampler: its sequence breakers cap the penalty at $\lambda b^{g-1-a}$ for loops whose longest breaker-free run has $g$ tokens. On eleven open models, 66\% of locked units with $g=6$ stay locked under DRY and 1\% with $g=8$. In free generation with this http URL, all 109 loops that survive DRY have $g\le 7$. We propose DRY-C, which adds a term that grows exponentially with the number of verbatim recurrences, up to its look-back window. With it, none of 720 structured-output generations looped to the length limit, and task completion stayed close to DRY's.

title: Martingale Posterior Cox Processes
abstract: Cox processes provide a principled Bayesian nonparametric framework for modeling event-based data through an underlying intensity function. However, existing inference methods for estimating the intensity typically rely on computationally expensive Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling or approximate inference techniques. In addition, to ensure tractability, these methods often define priors over indirect latent structures, making them challenging to interpret. In this paper, we introduce the Martingale Posterior Cox Process (MPCP), which recasts Bayesian intensity estimation as inference over unobserved events given the observed event history. This perspective avoids the need to define complex priors while retaining the flexibility of nonparametric modeling. We propose a scalable, GPU-friendly copula-based predictive update, and provide strong theoretical guarantees for the convergence of the predictive resampling algorithm. Empirically, we show that MPCP provides excellent performance in both simulations and real data at a fraction of the computational cost of competing Bayesian approaches.

title: Who Gets Unmasked? Sampler-Induced Bias in Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate by gradually unmasking a canvas, so their samplers decide not only which token to write but also when to commit it. We show that this second decision changes who appears in generated text, a sampler-induced bias on top of the model's own. Common commit rules, including LLaDA's default, commit the positions whose sampled tokens are most probable; this peeking favors majority options. To separate the sampler from the model, we read the model's belief about a fork, such as a protagonist's gender, in one forward pass, and show that this belief matches exact sampling from the model. Measured against it, peeking samplers on LLaDA and Dream amplify occupational gender stereotypes and collapse opinion distributions, and confidence-based ordering shifts gender-balanced occupations toward men, more so under faster parallel decoding. We propose Fork-First Sampling, which decides the fork before anything else is written: it follows the belief or any target distribution, improves fluency, and avoids the stories that remark on the protagonist's gender, which prompt-based fixes produce, at the cost of one forward pass. Fairness evaluations of dLLMs should report the commit rule.

title: Is User Calibration Still Necessary for Continuous Myoelectric Control? A Closed-Loop Comparison of Calibration-Free Controllers
comments: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering
subjects: Signal Processing (eess.SP); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: The need for user-specific calibration remains an often-cited barrier to widespread adoption of myoelectric control. Cross-user models trained on large multi-user datasets can now recognize gestures from unseen users without calibration, but they have been evaluated almost exclusively offline, leaving open whether calibration is still needed in closed-loop control. This study compared six calibration-free controllers, trained on 306 users of the EMG-EPN-612 dataset and used without any calibration data from the test participant, against three calibrated controllers in a closed-loop Fitts' law target-acquisition task with sixteen participants. The calibrated controllers achieved higher offline balanced accuracy (90.6% against 73.1% for the best controller of each paradigm), but completion rates did not differ significantly between paradigms, and the highest completion rate was achieved by a calibration-free controller. Calibrated controllers moved faster on successful acquisitions, partly because of their individually fitted speed mappings, though not significantly after correction for multiple comparisons. However, every calibration-free controller produced more direct and stable trajectories than every calibrated controller, even after adjusting for cursor speed. Offline accuracy did not predict completion rate across controllers or within participants, and across paradigms higher offline accuracy was associated with poorer trajectory quality in 15 of 16 participants. Without any calibration data from the end user, a model trained across a large population matched calibrated control in completion rate and exceeded it in trajectory quality. The offline accuracy gained through calibration should therefore not be taken as evidence of a closed-loop benefit.

title: Tilted Mondrian: Triage and Mitigation of Fine-grained Disparities in Conformal Prediction
abstract: Fairness in conformal prediction is often pursued through Mondrian calibration, which provides finite-sample coverage guarantees separately across groups. These guarantees, however, are coarse: substantial disparities can remain within finer strata. This coarse-to-fine fairness issue raises two questions: how severe can such disparities be, and how can they be mitigated? Aggregate disparities can depend on how groups are distributed across strata. For severity assessment, we introduce propensity standardization to examine the effect of population composition, and show how group composition can induce disagreement between aggregate and finer-stratum comparisons. For mitigation, we develop Tilted Mondrian to improve fairness compared to group-Mondrian at a finer level without additional model training. Tilted Mondrian retains groupwise coverage guarantees and mitigates coverage and prediction set size disparities within finer strata. Finally, we derive a method-agnostic bound that quantifies how much reduction in finer-stratum coverage disparity can be achieved.

title: Efficiency Measured in English: Tokeniser Coverage Bounds Small Language Models on Indic Scripts
subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computers and Society (cs.CY); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Small Language Models with quantisation and parameter-efficient adaptation are widely offered as the route to multilingual AI under compute constraints, and their efficiency is almost always reported as a single memory figure. We show that this figure is measured in English and does not transfer. Across a 131k-sentence corpus spanning eleven Indic scripts, TinyLlama-1.1B's tokeniser emits 1.34 subword tokens per Latin-script word and 22.60 per Kannada word. This is not inefficiency; it is absence. Its vocabulary contains 0% of Odia's codepoints, 1% of Telugu's and 2% of Kannada's, and for five of eleven scripts the measured fertility sits at the UTF-8 byte-fallback ceiling, on Odia at 99.6% of it, with 93.6% of emitted tokens being raw bytes. Because SentencePiece byte fallback never raises an unknown-token marker, this failure is entirely silent: TinyLlama's UNK rate is 0.0% on every script, including the one it reads as bytes. We further show that low fertility can indicate the opposite of efficiency: mBERT posts its best score anywhere (1.10 tokens/word, on Odia) while discarding 87.9% of the text as UNK. MuRIL, an Indic-vocabulary encoder with a fifth of TinyLlama's parameters, reads every script at 1.23-2.26 tokens/word with zero UNK and zero byte fallback. The binding constraint is the vocabulary, not the parameter count. The consequence is concrete: on a 2048-token context window, the same model gives an English user 1,528 words of usable context and a Kannada user 91.

title: The Missing Compliance Class: LLM Graders That Collapse Jailbreak Success, and a Free Check
comments: 29 pages, 6 figures, 17 tables. Code and labels: this https URL
subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Jailbreak papers report an attack success rate, the share of responses that deliver the harmful request, and read it as a property of the target model. We hold the target model, the prompts and the responses fixed and change only the grader. Three dense graders of 8B and 9B parameters, from three model families, move compliant responses to the neighbouring class, evasion, instead of scattering them across classes. One of them assigns the compliance label zero times in 900 responses. This class collapse also appears on new harmful requests, on a target model from a third family, and in a held-out 7B grader from a fourth family. Per-class label counts expose it at no cost and without human labels. The collapse decides how the rate behaves under a change of grader. On two corpora of 900 responses and eight graders, the compliance rate differs by a factor of 22 to 25, while the non-refusal rate differs by 18 to 23 percentage points. Without the three collapsing graders, compliance differs by a factor of 1.7 to 2.8 on all four corpora, and non-refusal still differs by 10 to 22 points. These results do not change when every grader is called once. We propose a reporting minimum that keeps the compliance rate and adds its per-class label counts and the named grader. Beside it goes the non-refusal rate, whose disagreement across graders is additive.

title: Measuring Data Diversity with Embeddings: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Diversity Measures
comments: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main). Code and data: this https URL
abstract: Diversity is a critical property of text corpora, with direct implications for training data curation, test set design, and model generalization. However, its measurement remains fragmented and poorly understood. Existing embedding-based diversity measures vary widely in how they are computed and can yield substantially different diversity scores on the same data, yet no systematic comparison of their empirical behaviour exists. We make two contributions toward addressing this gap. First, we present a taxonomy of 21 embedding-based diversity measures, organizing them into four families based on their underlying computations. Second, we introduce EmbDivBench, a benchmark that evaluates these measures along three conceptually distinct components (variety, balance and disparity) on both simulated and natural text data. Although Mean Pairwise Distance is the most commonly used measure, our experiments show that it is outperformed by several alternatives on the three diversity components, with Graph Entropy being the best choice overall. Lastly, we distil these findings into practical recommendations for diversity measure selection.

title: Query-Dependent Reading for Quantized Inner-Product Estimation: A Minimax Separation
comments: 66 pages
subjects: Information Theory (cs.IT); Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: We study quantization for inner-product estimation when storage and reading have separate budgets. In the static bit-probe model [Yao, 1981], an encoder stores $w$ bits about $x$ before seeing a query $y$, and a reader probes at most $r<w$ bits to estimate $x^\top y$. Both vectors lie in the $d$-dimensional Euclidean unit ball. Protocols may be randomized, and computation is unrestricted. Performance is measured by $d$ times the worst-case mean-squared error over $x,y$, averaged over protocol randomness. First, we show that query-independent reading cannot benefit from extra storage. Any such reader is equivalent to fully reading an $r$-bit message, even when later reads depend on previously returned bits. At fixed positive rates $W=w/d$ and $R=r/d$, the normalized minimax error converges to $1/(4^R-1)$, independent of $W$. The upper bound was already known [Ordentlich and Polyanskiy, 2025]. We prove the matching lower bound for arbitrary scalar decoders, extending the result for unbiased compressors [Safaryan et al., 2020]. Then, we show that query-dependent reading makes extra storage useful. We construct a two-batch protocol using Gaussian projections and random thresholds, with asymptotic normalized error at most $(\pi+o(1))/[4R\log(W/R)]$ as $W/R\to\infty$. At fixed $R$, this error vanishes as storage grows, giving an unbounded advantage over query-independent reading. We also prove a finite-dimensional lower bound for arbitrary encoders, decoders, and fully branching readers. In the doubly sparse regime $W/R\to\infty$ and $R\log(W/R)\to0$, it gives normalized error at least $(1-o(1))/[2R\log(W/R)]$. Thus, our protocol is optimal within a factor of $\pi/2$ in the leading constant.

title: Scalable and Adaptive Distribution Regression via Random Features
abstract: Distribution regression seeks to learn mappings from probability distributions to response variables and has emerged as a unifying framework for kernel methods, multi-instance learning, and set-valued learning. Despite its success, kernel-based distribution regression remains computationally expensive and sensitive to kernel choice, motivating scalable and adaptive representations. Building on random feature approximations, we develop a finite-sample analysis of Random Feature Distribution Regression (RaDR) under two-stage sampling.
